Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Driven magnetic 3D DNA walker coupled with CHA based on light-activatable hairpin: A dual-amplification strategy for ultrasensitive hantavirus RNA sensing.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Orthohantavirus dabieshanense (DBSV) is a newly emerging hantavirus and poses a potential threat to human health. Current detection methods based on polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays for other hantaviruses such as Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) may carry the risk of false negatives. This study aims to address the technical bottlenecks of low accuracy and insufficient sensitivity in current detection of DBSV. RESULTS: We developed a signal amplification strategy mediated by a photoactivated magnetic 3D DNA walker, which enables light-controllable fluorescence detection. Specifically, this fluorescence sensing platform introduces the catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA) technique for dual signal amplification. This system requires dual activation by UV irradiation and target RNA. Then, exonuclease III (Exo III) provides propulsion for the walking process to release a specific trigger strand, subsequently activating the CHA cycle and producing a fluorescent signal. Experimental results confirm that the system displays excellent selectivity and anti-interference ability, successfully distinguishing target sequences with single-base mismatch (SBM), double-base mismatch (DBM), and triple-base mismatch (TBM). Furthermore, the platform achieves a DBSV-RNA detection limit (LOD) of 30 fM with a linear range spanning 10-1-106 pM. The applicability of the method has been rigorously validated using human serum specimens. SIGNIFICANCE: This study provides a novel strategy for the application of spatiotemporally controllable DNA walkers in RNA detection, demonstrating considerable potential for early viral diagnosis and field monitoring.

analysis_zh.background: 正汉坦病毒 dabieshanense (DBSV) 是一种新出现的 汉坦病毒,可能威胁人类健康。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究采用光激活磁性3D DNA 行走器结合催化发卡组装(CHA),需紫外照射和目标 RNA 双重激活,并通过外切酶 III 驱动行走释放触发链,启动 CHA 荧光。

papers.title: In Silico Prediction and Structural Mapping of Linear B-Cell Epitopes in Andes Virus Glycoprotein as Potential Vaccine Candidates
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV), a pathogenic orthohantavirus associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, remains a public health concern because of its severe clinical outcomes and the absence of broadly approved vaccines for human use. The viral glycoprotein is a relevant antigenic target because of its surface localization and role in viral entry. This study aimed to identify and structurally map linear B-cell epitope candidates in the Andes virus glycoprotein using an immunoinformatics-based approach. The ANDV glycoprotein sequence was retrieved from UniProt, and linear B-cell epitopes were predicted using BepiPred 3.0 with a threshold of 0.030. Candidate peptides were further evaluated for antigenicity, allergenicity, and toxicity using VaxiJen v2.0, AllerTOP v2.1, and ToxinPred, respectively. The three-dimensional glycoprotein model was generated using AlphaFold, refined with GalaxyWEB, and validated using ERRAT and Ramachandran plot analysis. Five preliminary epitope candidates were identified, among which E1, E2, E3, and E4 met the antigenicity criterion. The refined structure showed favorable validation parameters, with an ERRAT score of 97.73 and 97.88% of residues in the favored Ramachandran region. Structural mapping indicated that E1 (EWRKKSDTTDTTNAASTTFE) and E2 (QTKTVNLRGT) were positioned on exposed surface regions, supporting their prioritization as the most promising candidates. E4 (PSTSSTDT) also showed potential, whereas E3 (HPRGEDHD), despite having the highest antigenicity score, appeared less structurally exposed. These findings provide preliminary computational evidence for surface-accessible linear B-cell epitope candidates in ANDV glycoprotein. However, experimental validation is required to confirm their immunological relevance.

Royhan Afnani1,3, Muhammad Fajrul Adi Syahputra1, Rangga Adhi Prastika2,3, Abdul Rahman Siregar1* 1Department of Biology, Faculty of Biology, Universitas Gadjah Mada, Yogyakarta, 55281, Indonesia 2Department of Nanotechnology Engineering, Faculty of Advanced Technology and Multidiscipline, Universitas Airlangga, Surabaya 60115, Indonesia. 3Drug and Vaccine Innovation Research Group, Virtual Research Center for Bioinformatics and Biotechnology, Surabaya, Indonesia *Corresponding author: ar.siregar@ugm.ac.id ARTICLE HISTORY Received: 16 Jun 2026 Revised: 21 Jul 2026 Accepted: 29 Jul 2026 Published: 30 Sep 2026 ABSTRACT Andes virus (ANDV), a pathogenic orthohantavirus associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, remains a public health concern because of its severe clinical outcomes and the absence of broadly approved vaccines for human use. Candidate peptides were evaluated for antigenicity, allergenicity, and toxicity using VaxiJen v2.0, AllerTOP v2.1, and ToxinPred, respectively. Surface-localized candidates were further assessed through molecular docking with a B-cell receptor structure using ClusPro 2.0, followed by binding free energy estimation using PRODIGY. Keywords: Andes virus; B-cell epitope; glycoprotein; immunoinformatics; structural mapping; candidate linear B-cell epitope Introduction A recent cluster of Andes virus infections associated with the cruise ship MV Hondius has heightened international concern regarding the public health significance of pathogenic orthohantaviruses (Koopmans et al., 2026). Andes virus (ANDV), a zoonotic pathogen within the genus Orthohantavirus and family Hantaviridae, typically infects humans through inhalation of aerosolized particles contaminated with urine, feces, or saliva from infected rodent reservoirs. Notably, ANDV is epidemiologically unique due to documented instances of limited person-to- person transmission, particularly among close contacts (Chediack et al., 2026; Martinez- Valdebenito et al., 2014). This transmission feature, combined with its association with severe cardiopulmonary disease, underscores the importance of ANDV for public health surveillance, outbreak preparedness, and vaccine development. ANDV is a primary etiological agent of hantavirus Journal of Tropical One Health Volume 1 (2026) Nariswari et al. h/ps://doi.org/10.22452/jtoh.vol1.1 Published by Tropical Infec5ous Disease Research and Educa5on Centre (TIDREC), Universi5 Malaya cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a severe disease marked by increased pulmonary vascular permeability, pulmonary edema, acute respiratory failure, and cardiogenic shock (Warner et al., 2025). While the incidence of HCPS is generally lower than that of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Old World hantaviruses, HCPS exhibits a substantially higher case-fatality rate, typically reported at 30–40% (Angulo et al., 2017; Barrera et al., 2025; Quarleri et al., 2026). Despite the clinical severity of ANDV infection, no specific antiviral therapy or widely approved vaccine is currently available for human use. This lack of medical countermeasures is particularly concerning given ecological disturbances, climate variability, and habitat changes that may influence rodent population dynamics and elevate the risk of human exposure to infected reservoirs (Moirano et al., 2024). Structurally, ANDV is an enveloped, negative- sense RNA virus with a tripartite genome consisting of small, medium, and large segments. The small segment encodes the nucleocapsid protein, the medium segment encodes a glycoprotein precursor processed into Gn and Gc, and the large segment encodes the RNA- dependent RNA polymerase (Beltrán-Ortiz et al., 2017). The envelope glycoproteins Gn and Gc are of particular interest for vaccine development because they are displayed on the virion surface and mediate host-cell attachment, receptor engagement, endocytic entry, and membrane fusion. Their surface exposure facilitates antibody recognition, supporting their selection as antigenic targets for epitope-based vaccine research (Banerjee & Mukhopadhyay, 2016; Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014). B-cell epitopes are specific antigenic regions recognized by antibodies and contribute to humoral immune responses (Caoili, 2022). In vaccine design, identifying B-cell epitopes is essential because antibody-mediated immunity and immunological memory are critical for protection against viral reinfection. Linear B-cell epitopes are particularly valuable in immunoinformatics-based screening, as they can be derived from the primary amino acid sequence, assessed for antigenicity and safety, and mapped onto three-dimensional antigen structures (Riswana & Punjungsari, 2025). However, sequence-based prediction alone does not adequately determine biological accessibility or immunogenic potential. Structural mapping is therefore required to establish whether predicted epitopes are located on solvent-exposed regions of the target protein, where they are more likely to be accessible to antibody binding (Afnani & Purnama, 2025; Francino-Urdaniz & Whitehead, 2021). Although B-cell epitope prediction, multiepitope vaccine design, and structural evaluation have been applied in viral vaccine- related studies, including hantavirus targets, most previous hantavirus immunoinformatics studies have emphasized broad whole-proteome screening or multiepitope vaccine construct design rather than a focused prioritization of linear B-cell epitopes derived specifically from the ANDV glycoprotein (Abdulla et al., 2021). The novelty of the present study therefore does not rely on the use of individual computational tools, which are well-established in immunoinformatics research, but on the ANDV- specific integration of linear B-cell epitope prediction, antigenicity and safety screening, three-dimensional structural mapping, and molecular docking with a B-cell receptor structure for candidate prioritization. This integrated approach allows predicted epitopes to be evaluated not only on the basis of sequence-level epitope propensity, but also according to their predicted antigenicity, safety profile, structural localization, and interaction potential with an antigen-recognition model. Such a focused framework is particularly relevant for glycoprotein antigens, in which not all sequence- predicted epitopes are necessarily exposed or available for antibody recognition on the folded protein surface. Therefore, this study aimed to identify and prioritize linear B-cell epitope candidates in the Andes virus glycoprotein through an integrated immunoinformatics approach combining sequence-based prediction, antigenicity and safety screening, three-dimensional structural mapping, and molecular docking with a B-cell receptor structure. Candidate epitopes were further assessed for antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, structural localization, and predicted BCR-binding affinity. The results provide preliminary computational evidence for prioritized surface-accessible linear B-cell epitope candidates that may inform future experimental evaluation for Andes virus vaccine-associated or diagnostic applications. However, as this study is Journal of Tropical One Health Volume 1 (2026) Nariswari et al. h/ps://doi.org/10.22452/jtoh.vol1.1 Published by Tropical Infec5ous Disease Research and Educa5on Centre (TIDREC), Universi5 Malaya entirely computational, the predicted epitopes should be regarded as potential candidates requiring further experimental validation through in vitro and in vivo studies. Materials and Methods Retrieval and Curation of Andes Virus Glycoprotein Sequence The ANDV glycoprotein sequence was retrieved from the UniProt Knowledgebase using the taxonomic identifier and protein accession as search criteria. The UniProt entry Q9E006, annotated as ANDV glycoprotein and consisting of 1138 amino acids, was selected as the reference sequence for downstream analysis (Shimizu et al., 2013). The FASTA sequence and associated metadata, including accession number, organism name, protein length, and database source, were recorded to ensure sequence traceability and reproducibility. UniProtKB provides curated protein sequence and functional annotation resources, supporting its use as a primary source for protein sequence retrieval. Linear B-Cell Epitope Prediction Linear B-cell epitope prediction was performed using BepiPred 3.0, a sequence-based epitope prediction tool developed for identifying residues with potential B-cell epitope propensity (Clifford et al., 2022). The higher-confidence prediction option was selected. In this study, a threshold of ≥0.030 was used as a sequence-specific operational cutoff based on the score distribution observed across the ANDV glycoprotein. This cutoff was selected to balance epitope recovery and prediction stringency. Higher cutoff values retained only a very limited number of short epitope regions and reduced the ability to capture biologically plausible contiguous peptide segments, whereas lower cutoff values increased the inclusion of low-scoring regions that may represent less reliable predictions. Antigenicity, Allergenicity, and Toxicity Screening The predicted linear B-cell epitope candidates were further evaluated for antigenicity, allergenicity, and toxicity. Antigenicity was assessed using VaxiJen v2.0 with a threshold value of 0.400; peptides with antigenicity scores above this threshold were considered potentially antigenic (Afnani, Kharisma, et al., 2026). VaxiJen is an alignment-independent antigen prediction server that classifies antigens based on the physicochemical properties of protein sequences (Doytchinova & Flower, 2007). Allergenicity was predicted using AllerTOP v2.1, and only peptides classified as non-allergenic were retained. AllerTOP is an alignment-free allergenicity prediction server based on physicochemical properties and machine-learning classification (Dimitrov et al., 2014). Toxicity was evaluated using ToxinPred, and peptides predicted as non-toxic were prioritized for further structural mapping. ToxinPred is designed to classify peptides as toxic or non-toxic based on computational sequence-derived features (Rathore et al., 2024). Prediction, Refinement, and 3D Structure Validation The three-dimensional (3D) structure of the Andes virus glycoprotein was predicted using the AlphaFold Server (Kovalevskiy et al., 2024; Prastika et al., 2026). The predicted structure was then refined using the GalaxyWEB server to improve local structural geometry and reduce potential modeling artifacts. The refined model was validated using structure quality assessment parameters (Ko et al., 2012). The ERRAT score was calculated using the Structure Validation Server, and stereochemical quality was assessed using Ramachandran plot analysis through RamPlot (Afnani, Emilia, et al., 2026; Laskowski et al., 2013). The validated model was subsequently used as the structural template for mapping the selected linear B-cell epitope candidates. Structural Mapping and Visualization of Linear B-Cell Epitope Candidates The selected linear B-cell epitope candidates were mapped onto the refined 3D structure of the ANDV glycoprotein using PyMOL under an academic license. Epitope positions were identified based on their amino acid coordinates in the full-length glycoprotein sequence and visualized on the 3D model using distinct colors. Both cartoon and surface representations were generated to assess the spatial distribution and surface exposure of each candidate epitope (Riswana & Punjungsari, 2025). Epitope candidates located on surface-exposed regions were prioritized because B-cell epitopes are more likely to be accessible to antibody recognition when positioned on the external surface of the antigen. In contrast, epitopes located within Journal of Tropical One Health Volume 1 (2026) Nariswari et al. h/ps://doi.org/10.22452/jtoh.vol1.1 Published by Tropical Infec5ous Disease Research and Educa5on Centre (TIDREC), Universi5 Malaya buried, transmembrane, or structurally uncertain regions were interpreted with caution and were not prioritized for further analysis. Molecular Docking with B-Cell ReceptorThe prioritized linear B-cell epitopes, were further evaluated through molecular docking with the B- cell receptor (BCR). The BCR structure was obtained from the RCSB Protein Data Bank using PDB ID 5IFH (Riswana & Punjungsari, 2025). Molecular docking was performed using the ClusPro 2.0, with BCR designated as the receptor and each epitope peptide as the ligand (Arapa et al., 2026). The best-ranked docking complex from each epitope-BCR interaction was selected for further evaluation. The predicted binding free energy (ΔG) of each complex was then assessed using the PRODIGY web server, where more negative ΔG values indicate stronger predicted binding affinity (Xue et al., 2016). The resulting docking complexes were visualized using PyMOL to examine the interaction orientation and spatial positioning of each epitope on the BCR surface. This analysis is significant because B-cell epitopes represent antigenic regions recognized by antibodies and may serve as preliminary targets for vaccine- associated evaluation, immunodiagnostic development, and immune-reactivity assessment. analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) is a pathogenic orthohantavirus that causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome with severe outcomes and currently lacks approved human vaccines, making it a public‑health concern.
analysis.methods: The study retrieved the ANDV glycoprotein sequence from UniProt and predicted linear B‑cell epitopes using BepiPred 3.0 (threshold 0.030); candidate peptides were screened for antigenicity, allergenicity, and toxicity with VaxiJen v2.0, AllerTOP v2.1, and ToxinPred; a 3‑D glycoprotein model was built with AlphaFold, refined by GalaxyWEB, and validated via ERRAT and Ramachandran analysis; surface‑exposed epitopes were further docked to a B‑cell receptor using ClusPro 2.0 and binding free energies estimated with PRODIGY.
analysis.results: Five preliminary epitopes were identified, of which E1, E2, E3, and E4 met antigenicity criteria; the refined model showed an ERRAT score of 97.73 % and 97.88 % residues in favored Ramachandran regions; E1 (EWRKKSDTTDTTNAASTTFE) and E2 (QTKTVNLRGT) were surface‑exposed, E4 (PSTSSTDT) showed potential, while E3 was less exposed; docking yielded predicted binding free energies of –10.0, –9.4, and –9.1 kcal/mol for E1, E2, and E4 respectively.
analysis.contribution: The work provides preliminary computational evidence of surface‑accessible linear B‑cell epitopes in the ANDV glycoprotein, offering candidate targets for future vaccine design and serological tool development.
analysis.limitations: Findings are based solely on in‑silico predictions; experimental validation of antigenicity, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy is required.

papers.title: Differential PCDH1 usage by Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal hantaviruses
papers.abstract: Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus are hantaviruses associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), but their cellular entry receptors have not been defined. We used replication-competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing hantavirus Gn/Gc glycoprotein complexes to compare entry by these viruses, the Old World rodent-borne Dabieshan virus and Tigray virus, and the shrew-borne Cao Bang virus and Amga virus. All six Gn/Gc complexes supported infection of primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells, with virus-specific efficiencies and kinetics. Genetic ablation of protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) reduced infection mediated by Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus Gn/Gc in human osteosarcoma and endothelial cells, whereas PCDH1 re-expression restored susceptibility. Both viruses were captured by a soluble PCDH1 protein comprising the first two extracellular cadherin domains. Infection was also inhibited by a soluble decoy containing the first cadherin domain, and by an antibody specific to that domain, indicating that the first PCDH1 cadherin domain mediates viral engagement. Black Creek Canal Gn/Gc-bearing rVSVs incorporated less Gn/Gc and showed lower apparent capture by PCDH1 than Laguna Negra virus and Andes virus Gn/Gc-bearing particles, even after normalization for glycoprotein abundance. In contrast, PCDH1 depletion did not detectably alter infection mediated by the other four hantavirus Gn/Gc complexes. Thus, Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus use PCDH1 for efficient entry but differ in apparent receptor engagement and responses to PCDH1-directed inhibitors, whereas all six viruses are potently neutralized by the broadly reactive Gn/Gc-directed antibody ADI-42898.

All six Gn/Gc complexes supported infection of primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells, with virus-specific efficiencies and kinetics. Genetic ablation of protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) reduced infection mediated by Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus Gn/Gc in human osteosarcoma and endothelial cells, whereas PCDH1 re-expression restored susceptibility. Both viruses were captured by a soluble PCDH1 protein comprising the first two extracellular cadherin domains. Infection was also inhibited by a soluble decoy containing the first cadherin domain, and by an antibody specific to that domain, indicating that the first PCDH1 cadherin domain mediates viral engagement. Black Creek Canal Gn/Gc-bearing rVSVs incorporated less Gn/Gc and showed lower apparent capture by PCDH1 than Laguna Negra virus and Andes virus Gn/Gc-bearing particles, even after normalization for glycoprotein abundance. In contrast, PCDH1 depletion did not detectably alter infection mediated by the other four hantavirus Gn/Gc complexes. Thus, Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus use PCDH1 for efficient entry but differ in apparent receptor engagement and responses to PCDH1-directed inhibitors, whereas all six viruses are potently neutralized by the broadly reactive Gn/Gc-directed antibody ADI-42898.

Using BSL2-compatible rVSVs bearing hantavirus glycoproteins, we 48 show that Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus, two hantaviruses 49 associated with human cardiopulmonary disease, used protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) for 50 efficient entry into human cells. PCDH1-directed inhibitors blocked infection, but the two 51 viruses differed in apparent receptor engagement and inhibitor sensitivity, showing that 52 PCDH1 usage is not uniform even among closely related viruses. A broadly reactive antibody 56 neutralized every virus in the study panel, supporting conserved viral glycoprotein 57 surfaces as therapeutic targets when receptor usage is diverse or unknown. 58 59 Introduction 60 Entry of enveloped viruses into host cells is a major determinant of tissue tropism and 61 cross-species transmission(1). Mammalian hantaviruses (family Hantaviridae, order 62 Elliovirales) are emerging zoonotic pathogens that cause severe, often fatal illness in 63 humans after transmission from chronically infected small-mammal reservoirs, 64 manifesting as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia and 65 hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in the Americas (2, 3). The public health 66 significance of hantaviruses is underscored by their recurring emergence, including a 67 multi-country HCPS outbreak in April-May 2026, which involved limited secondary 68 transmission and resulted in three reported deaths (4–6). Despite significant morbidity 69 and high case-fatality rates approaching 40% for HCPS, no FDA-approved 70 prophylactics or antiviral therapeutics are currently available (7). Cellular entry of 71 hantaviruses is orchestrated entirely by the envelope glycoprotein complex Gn/Gc (8, 72 9). Gn and Gc are synthesized as a single polyprotein precursor encoded by the 73 medium (M) genomic segment, co-translationally cleaved by cellular signal peptidases, 74 and assemble into spike-like tetramers of Gn/Gc heterodimers on the virion envelope 75 (8–11)These glycoproteins coordinate entry: the membrane-distal Gn subunit likely 76 mediates host receptor engagement, while the class II fusion protein Gc drives low-pH- 77 dependent membrane fusion within late endosomes envelope (8–12) Despite the 78 identification of dozens of hantavirus species across rodent and insectivore hosts 79 globally, host entry receptors and neutralization vulnerabilities for most divergent 80 species remain undefined (10, 13, 14). 81 Candidate hantavirus attachment factors and receptors initially identified through 82 antibody blockade, ligand competition, or in vitro binding assays include β1, β2, and β3 83 integrins, decay-accelerating factor (DAF/CD55), and gC1qR complement receptor (15– 84 19). However, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated loss-of-function screens in human 85 microvascular endothelial cells, a primary in vivo target cell type, demonstrated that 86 knockout of ITGB1, ITGB3, or DAF had little or no effect on infection by a panel of 87 virulent hantaviruses, indicating that these molecules are dispensable for endothelial 88 cell entry (20). Unbiased haploid-genetic screening instead identified protocadherin-1 89 (PCDH1) as an essential entry receptor for Andes virus (ANDV, Orthohantavirus 90 andesense) and Sin Nombre virus (SNV, Orthohantavirus sinnombreense): its 91 membrane-distal extracellular cadherin domain 1 (EC1) directly binds Gn/Gc, and 92 genetic ablation of PCDH1 in cultured cells and Syrian hamsters protects against ANDV 93 infection and lethal disease (21). Point mutations within the EC1 contact surface disrupt 94 infection, establishing PCDH1-EC1 as the functional interface (22). Although PCDH1 95 usage has been established for multiple hantaviruses, the glycoprotein determinants 96 that govern receptor recognition across divergent lineages remain incompletely defined 97 (20–22). PCDH1 usage has also been documented beyond the canonical New World 98 clade, including in vole- and mole-borne viruses (23), but its distribution across other 99 rodent- and shrew-borne clades has yet to be fully mapped. 100 Gn/Gc amino acid sequences differ by roughly 40-60% between hantavirus lineages, 101 and most glycoprotein-directed monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) raised or isolated against 102 one species show little heterologous neutralization (24, 25). Consequently, broadly 103 active entry inhibitors may need to target either conserved virus-receptor interfaces or 104 rare, functionally constrained epitopes on the viral spike (11, 21, 24, 25). On the host 105 side, the EC1-specific mAb-3305, soluble histidine-tagged PCDH1 ectodomain proteins 106 containing EC1-2 or EC1-4 (sEC1-2, sEC1-4), and a human Fc-tagged soluble EC1 107 decoy (EC1-Fc) block PCDH1-Gn/Gc engagement and neutralize PCDH1-dependent 108 viruses (21–23). Conversely, targeting conserved epitopes on the viral spike can 109 provide broad neutralization across clades. In particular, mAb-42898, isolated from a 110 Puumala virus (PUUV, Orthohantavirus puumalaense)-convalescent individual, binds a 111 quaternary epitope bridging the Gn capping loop and Gc fusion loops, neutralizes 112 multiple HCPS- and HFRS-causing viruses, and protects rodents against lethal 113 challenge (24, 26). Evaluating an expanded panel of uncharacterized Gn/Gc complexes 114 against both receptor-targeted and spike-targeted approaches can reveal conserved 115 viral vulnerabilities and inform the development of broadly active therapeutics. 116 Functional entry studies of less-characterized hantaviruses are constrained by the 117 limited availability of cultivable isolates and the requirement for biosafety level 3 or 4 118 (BSL3/4) containment for pathogenic hantaviruses (10). Here, we generated replication- 119 competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) expressing an enhanced 120 green fluorescent protein (eGFP) reporter and bearing codon-optimized Gn/Gc 121 complexes from six ecologically and phylogenetically distinct hantaviruses: the HCPS- 122 associated Black Creek Canal virus (BCCV, Orthohantavirus nigrorivense; carried by 123 Hispid cotton rat) (27) and Laguna Negra virus (LANV, Orthohantavirus mamorense; 124 small vesper mouse) (28); the Old World rodent-borne Dabieshan virus (DBSV, 125 Orthohantavirus dabieshanense; Chinese white-bellied rat) (29) and Tigray virus (TIGV, 126 Orthohantavirus tigrayense; Ethiopian white-footed mouse) (30, 31); the shrew-borne 127 Cao Bang virus (CBNV, Orthohantavirus caobangense; Chinese mole shrew) (32) and 128 Amga virus (MGAV, Orthohantavirus artybashense; Laxmann's shrew) (33, 34). This 129 panel includes viruses with distinct and incompletely defined zoonotic relevance. TIGV 130 circulates in peridomestic rodents in Ethiopia, where orthohantavirus-reactive antibodies 131 were detected in human sera (35). DBSV is genetically related to the prototypic HFRS- 132 causing Hantaan virus (HTNV), whereas CBNV and MGAV are shrew-borne viruses 133 with no established association with human disease (13, 29). 134 BCCV and LANV are particularly notable because authentic isolates exist for both, and 135 each has been studied extensively in epidemiologic, reservoir, and animal-model 136 settings. BCCV persists asymptomatically with horizontal transmission in its natural 137 reservoir but is uniformly lethal in immunosuppressed Syrian hamsters (36–38), 138 whereas LANV causes HCPS across South America and lethal pulmonary disease in 139 Turkish hamsters (39). Despite this substantial body of work, the receptor requirements 140 of both viruses remain undefined: BCCV entry was last examined before any hantavirus 141 receptor was identified (40) and neither virus has been tested for PCDH1 dependence. 142 To recover replication-competent rVSVs bearing Old World rodent-borne and shrew- 143 borne glycoproteins, we engineered Gn/Gc constructs using previously established 144 HTNV-based rescue-enhancing substitutions (23, 41). Here we show that all six Gn/Gc 145 complexes mediate infection of human microvascular endothelial cells, consistent with 146 systematic pseudotype screens showing that receptor-binding proteins from diverse 147 animal viruses can function broadly in human cells (1). CRISPR/Cas9-based genetic 148 depletion and cDNA complementation in human cells demonstrated that infection 149 mediated by glycoproteins of BCCV and LANV—but not those of DBSV, TIGV, CBNV, 150 or MGAV—depends on PCDH1. Concordantly, BCCV and LANV glycoproteins bound 151 soluble PCDH1 with different efficiencies in sEC1-2 capture ELISAs, were competitively 152 blocked at this interface by EC1-specific mAb-3305, and were neutralized by EC1-Fc 153 and mAb-3305 in endothelial cell infection assays. Finally, ADI-42898 bound all six 154 Gn/Gc-bearing particles and neutralized them with variable potency that correlated with 155 naturally occurring amino acid variation at epitope sites corresponding to PUUV 156 residues Q98, E750, and E768. Together, our findings expand the known diversity of 157 hantavirus receptor usage and define human endothelial cell susceptibility and antibody 158 sensitivity profiles across an expanded spectrum of hantavirus glycoproteins. 159 Results 160 Gn/Gc complexes from divergent rodent- and shrew-borne hantaviruses mediate 161 infection of human endothelial cells 162 We evaluated whether Gn/Gc glycoproteins from six phylogenetically and ecologically 163 distinct hantaviruses could mediate infection of human endothelial cells. The panel 164 included the New World rodent-borne viruses Black Creek Canal virus (BCCV) and 165 Laguna Negra virus (LANV), the Old World rodent-borne viruses Dabieshan virus 166 (DBSV) and Tigray virus (TIGV), and the shrew-borne Cao Bang virus (CBNV) and 167 Amga virus (MGAV) (Fig. 1A). Although cell culture isolates are available for BCCV and 168 LANV (27, 28), authenticated isolates have not been reported for DBSV, TIGV, CBNV 169 or MGAV, which are known from viral sequences recovered from reservoir tissues. 170 To examine Gn/Gc-mediated entry under BSL2 conditions, we generated replication- 171 competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) in which the native VSV G 172 open reading frame was replaced with the Gn/Gc open reading frame from LANV, 173 BCCV, DBSV, CBNV, TIGV, or MGAV. An enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) 174 reporter was included in the first transcriptional unit to permit quantitation of infected 175 cells (Fig. 1B, top). Consistent with established rVSV rescue strategies for Old World 176 rodent-borne, mole-, and shrew-borne viruses, constructs from DBSV, CBNV, TIGV, 177 and MGAV contained the Hantaan virus (HTNV)-derived rescue-enhancing substitutions 178 I532K in the Gn cytoplasmic tail and S1094L in the membrane-proximal stem of Gc 179 ectodomain (23, 41) (Fig. 1B bottom). In selected constructs, adjacent residues were 180 also replaced with their HTNV counterparts. These modifications promote plasma- 181 membrane localization and rVSV incorporation of HTNV Gn/Gc and lie outside the 182 receptor-binding interface and the mapped neutralizing-antibody epitopes evaluated 183 here. 184 Recovery of rVSV-BCCV required an S430C substitution. Because cysteine is highly 185 conserved at the corresponding position among mammalian hantaviruses, the serine 186 reported in the deposited BCCV GenBank sequence may reflect a sequencing error 187 rather than authentic viral variation. Nanopore sequencing of rescued rVSV stocks 188 identified no additional nonsynonymous changes beyond the engineered substitutions, 189 except for G485R in rVSV-MGAV. This substitution has also been observed during 190 rescue of rVSV bearing the related Kenkeme virus Gn/Gc (23) but not for most other 191 hantavirus Gn/Gc proteins (20, 21, 42–44). G485, the terminal residue of the Gn 192 ectodomain, is highly conserved among hantaviruses; however, the functional 193 consequences of the G485R substitution remain unknown. 194 We then measured infection of primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial 195 cells (HPMECs) over 48 h at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 1 (Fig. 1C and D). Virus 196 inputs were normalized using titers determined in permissive Huh-7.5.1 cells. At 12 h 197 postinfection (hpi), rVSV-LANV and rVSV-DBSV infection approached or exceeded that 198 of the rVSV-ANDV control, with approximately 30-40% of cells becoming eGFP positive 199 (Fig. 1C and D). Infection by these viruses and by rVSV-ANDV peaked between 24 and 200 36 hpi, reaching approximately 70-90% eGFP positive cells (Fig. 1D). In contrast, rVSV- 201 BCCV infection was only minimally detectable at 12 hpi, at approximately 4%, and 202 increased to a plateau of approximately 20% by 24 hpi (Fig. 1D). rVSV-CBNV, rVSV- 203 TIGV, and rVSV-MGAV produced slower and lower-level infection, becoming readily 204 detectable only at 48 hpi, when approximately 4-8% of cells were eGFP positive (Fig. 205 1C and D). 206 Thus, all six Gn/Gc complexes mediated infection of primary human endothelial cells 207 but differed substantially in infection efficiency and kinetics. These data establish human 208 endothelial-cell entry competence for LANV and BCCV Gn/Gc and provide functional 209 evidence that the Gn/Gc complexes of DBSV, TIGV, CBNV, and MGAV can mediate 210 cellular entry. 211 BCCV and LANV Gn/Gc-mediated infection depends on PCDH1 212 We next tested whether the Gn/Gc complexes in this panel require PCDH1 for entry. 213 Wild-type (WT), PCDH1-knockout cells transduced with empty vector (KO + EV), and 214 PCDH1-knockout cells complemented with PCDH1 cDNA (KO + PCDH1) were infected 215 with the indicated rVSVs. These genetic backgrounds in previously validated human 216 osteosarcoma U2OS and telomerase-immortalized human microvascular endothelial 217 (TIME) cell systems enable distinction between PCDH1-dependent and PCDH1- 218 independent hantavirus entry pathways (20–23). 219 In U2OS cells, PCDH1 ablation reduced infection by rVSV-BCCV and rVSV-LANV by 220 approximately 50-60%, similar to the reduction observed for the PCDH1-dependent 221 rVSV-ANDV control (Fig. 2A). PCDH1 re-expression restored rVSV-LANV and rVSV- 222 ANDV infection. Infection by rVSV-BCCV also increased after PCDH1 223 complementation, reaching levels above those observed in WT cells. In contrast, 224 PCDH1 status had little or no effect on infection by rVSV-DBSV, rVSV-CBNV, rVSV- 225 TIGV, and rVSV-MGAV, paralleling the well-established PCDH1-independent infection 226 of rVSV-HTNV. 227 We confirmed this phenotype in TIME cells, providing an endothelial cell context 228 relevant to hantavirus tropism. In these cells, PCDH1 knockout reduced rVSV-BCCV 229 and rVSV-LANV infection by approximately 75% relative to WT cells, comparable to the 230 reduction observed for rVSV-ANDV (Fig. 2B). rVSV-HTNV infection was not 231 significantly affected by PCDH1 knockout. analysis.background: Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), but their cellular entry receptors have not been defined (A1).
analysis.methods: The authors generated replication‑competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing the Gn/Gc glycoprotein complexes of six hantaviruses and used these to assess entry into human cells (A2).
analysis.results: All six Gn/Gc complexes infected primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells with virus‑specific efficiencies (A3). Genetic ablation of protocadherin‑1 (PCDH1) reduced infection by Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal viruses, and re‑expression restored susceptibility (A4). Soluble PCDH1 ectodomain and an EC1‑specific antibody blocked infection, indicating that the first PCDH1 cadherin domain mediates viral engagement (A5‑A6). PCDH1 depletion did not affect entry of the other four hantavirus Gn/Gc complexes (A8).
analysis.contribution: The study shows that Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal viruses use PCDH1 for efficient entry, but differ in receptor engagement and sensitivity to PCDH1‑directed inhibitors, highlighting heterogeneity in receptor usage among hantaviruses (A9).
analysis.limitations: Only in vitro recombinant‑VSV entry assays were performed; no animal infection models or clinical data were presented, and quantitative details such as virus titers or replication kinetics were not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal hantaviruses cause HCPS but their entry receptors were unknown (A1). Methods: Researchers used replication‑competent rVSVs bearing hantavirus Gn/Gc to test entry into human cells (A2). Results: All six Gn/Gc complexes infected primary human pulmonary endothelial cells; PCDH1 knockout reduced infection by Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal viruses, which was rescued by PCDH1 re‑expression, and soluble PCDH1 or EC1‑specific antibody blocked entry, while the other four viruses were PCDH1‑independent (A3‑A6, A8). Contribution: The work demonstrates PCDH1 as a functional receptor for these two viruses but reveals variability in receptor engagement and inhibitor sensitivity (A9). Limitations: The study is limited to in vitro rVSV assays without animal or clinical validation, and quantitative infection metrics are not provided.

papers.title_zh: Laguna Negra 与 Black Creek Canal 病毒对 PCDH1 的差异性利用 汉坦病毒es

analysis_zh.background: Laguna Negra 病毒和 Black Creek Canal 病毒导致 汉坦病毒心肺综合征(HCPS),但其细胞进入受体尚未确定 (A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者构建了携带六种 汉坦病毒 的 Gn/Gc 糖蛋白复合体的可复制重组水疱性口炎病毒 (rVSV),并利用这些病毒评估其进入人类细胞的情况 (A2)。
analysis_zh.results: 所有六种 Gn/Gc 复合体均以病毒特异的效率感染了初代人肺微血管内皮细胞 (A3)。基因敲除 protocadherin‐1 (PCDH1) 可降低 Laguna Negra 与 Black Creek Canal 病毒的感染,重新表达则恢复易感性 (A4)。可溶性 PCDH1 细胞外结构域及针对 EC1 的特异性抗体阻断了感染,表明首个 PCDH1 链粘蛋白结构域介导病毒结合 (A5‐A6)。PCDH1 缺失对其他四种 汉坦病毒 Gn/Gc 复合体的进入无影响 (A8)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究表明 Laguna Negra 与 Black Creek Canal 病毒利用 PCDH1 实现高效进入,但在受体结合方式和对 PCDH1 定向抑制剂的敏感性上存在差异,凸显 汉坦病毒 之间受体使用的异质性 (A9)。

papers.title: Vaccines for the prevention of hantavirus fevers: An overview of results and development prospects
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION. Hantavirus fevers, known as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, are natural focal diseases with a wide range of clinical manifestations. The causative agents are members of the genus Orthohantavirus , whose natural reservoirs are rodents of various species. There is currently no etiotropic therapy for these diseases. Specific prophylaxis through vaccination is available only in the DPRK, the Republic of Korea, and the People's Republic of China. An important objective is to provide the Russian and European markets with a relevant vaccine for HFRS prevention. Such a vaccine should be developed based on both time-proven approaches and the experience of modern developments. AIM. Analysis of the use of existing hantavirus vaccines and the specific features of vaccines under development, as well as assessment of the prospects for creating vaccines for HFRS prevention in the Russian Federation. DISCUSSION. All commercially available vaccine preparations are inactivated whole-virion vaccines based on the Hantaan and Seoul viruses. The effectiveness of these preparations varies, but a significant reduction in the incidence rate in regions with mass vaccination and a low incidence of adverse events have been noted. Several inactivated whole-virion vaccines based on relevant orthohantavirus strains have been developed in Russia. Some of these developments have successfully completed preclinical studies. The spectrum of hantavirus vaccine preparations under development includes subunit vaccines, vaccines based on virus-like particles (VLPs) and viral vectors, DNA vaccines, and mRNA vaccines. The primary immunogens are the surface glycoproteins Gn and Gc of hantaviruses. The closest to implementation into clinical practice are the DNA vaccines based on the Puumala and Hantaan viruses, which have undergone clinical trials (phase I). CONCLUSIONS. No vaccine for the prevention of hantavirus infections developed using virus-like particles (VLPs), viral vectors, or nucleic acids (DNA or mRNA) has undergone a full cycle of clinical trials or been licensed worldwide. On the contrary, well-established traditional technologies for manufacturing inactivated vaccines and their time-proven effectiveness provide a basis for their real prospects of practical application in the Russian Federation and other European countries.

papers.full_text: Вакцины для профилактики хантавирусных лихорадок: обзор результатов и перспектив разработок https://doi.org/10.30895/2221-996X-2026-26-3-324-335 Резюме ВВЕДЕНИЕ. Хантавирусные лихорадки, регистрируемые как геморрагическая лихорадка с почечным синдромом (ГЛПС) на Евроазиатском и хантавирусный пульмональный синдром (ХПС) на Американском континентах, представляют собой природно-очаговые болезни с широким диапазоном клинических проявлений. Возбудители — представители рода Orthohantavirus, резервуаром которых в природе являются грызуны различных видов. Этиотропной терапии хантавирусных лихорадок в настоящее время не существует. Специфическая профилактика в форме вакцинации проводится только в КНДР, Республике Корее и КНР. Важной задачей является обеспечение российского и европейского рынка актуальной вакциной для профилактики ГЛПС. Противохантавирусная вакцина должна разрабатываться как с учетом подходов, доказавших временем свою эффективность, так и опыта современных разработок. ЦЕЛЬ. Анализ применения существующих хантавирусных и особенностей разрабатываемых вакцин, а также оценка перспектив создания вакцин для профилактики ГЛПС в Российской Федерации. ОБСУЖДЕНИЕ. Все коммерчески доступные вакцинные препараты являются инактивированными цельновирионными вакцинами на основе вирусов Хантаан и Сеул. Эффективность этих препаратов различается, но отмечается существенное снижение заболеваемости в регионах с массовой вакцинацией и низкая частота побочных явлений. В России разработаны несколько инактивированных цельновирионных вакцин на основе актуальных штаммов ортохантавирусов. Некоторые из разработок успешно прошли доклинические испытания. Спектр разрабатываемых хантавирусных вакцинных препаратов представлен субъединичными вакцинами, вакцинами на основе вирусоподобных частиц и вирусных векторов, ДНК- и мРНК-вакцин. В качестве основных иммуногенов используются поверхностные гликопротеины Gn и Gc хантавирусов. Наиболее близко к внедрению в медицинскую практику оказались ДНК-вакцины на основе вирусов Пуумала и Хантаан, прошедшие клинические исследования (фаза I). ЗАКЛЮЧЕНИЕ. Ни один вакцинный препарат для профилактики хантавирусных инфекций, разработанный на основе вирусоподобных частиц, вирусных векторов, нуклеиновых кислот, не прошел полного цикла клинических испытаний и не лицензирован в мире. Напротив, отлаженные традиционные технологии изготовления инактивированных вакцин и их доказанная временем эффективность обусловливают реальные перспективы их практического применения в России и других европейских странах. full_text_sections.full_text: Вакцины для профилактики хантавирусных лихорадок: обзор результатов и перспектив разработок https://doi.org/10.30895/2221-996X-2026-26-3-324-335 Резюме ВВЕДЕНИЕ. Хантавирусные лихорадки, регистрируемые как геморрагическая лихорадка с почечным синдромом (ГЛПС) на Евроазиатском и хантавирусный пульмональный синдром (ХПС) на Американском континентах, представляют собой природно-очаговые болезни с широким диапазоном клинических проявлений. Возбудители — представители рода Orthohantavirus, резервуаром которых в природе являются грызуны различных видов. Этиотропной терапии хантавирусных лихорадок в настоящее время не существует. Специфическая профилактика в форме вакцинации проводится только в КНДР, Республике Корее и КНР. Важной задачей является обеспечение российского и европейского рынка актуальной вакциной для профилактики ГЛПС. Противохантавирусная вакцина должна разрабатываться как с учетом подходов, доказавших временем свою эффективность, так и опыта современных разработок. ЦЕЛЬ. Анализ применения существующих хантавирусных и особенностей разрабатываемых вакцин, а также оценка перспектив создания вакцин для профилактики ГЛПС в Российской Федерации. ОБСУЖДЕНИЕ. Все коммерчески доступные вакцинные препараты являются инактивированными цельновирионными вакцинами на основе вирусов Хантаан и Сеул. Эффективность этих препаратов различается, но отмечается существенное снижение заболеваемости в регионах с массовой вакцинацией и низкая частота побочных явлений. В России разработаны несколько инактивированных цельновирионных вакцин на основе актуальных штаммов ортохантавирусов. Некоторые из разработок успешно прошли доклинические испытания. Спектр разрабатываемых хантавирусных вакцинных препаратов представлен субъединичными вакцинами, вакцинами на основе вирусоподобных частиц и вирусных векторов, ДНК- и мРНК-вакцин. В качестве основных иммуногенов используются поверхностные гликопротеины Gn и Gc хантавирусов. Наиболее близко к внедрению в медицинскую практику оказались ДНК-вакцины на основе вирусов Пуумала и Хантаан, прошедшие клинические исследования (фаза I). ЗАКЛЮЧЕНИЕ. Ни один вакцинный препарат для профилактики хантавирусных инфекций, разработанный на основе вирусоподобных частиц, вирусных векторов, нуклеиновых кислот, не прошел полного цикла клинических испытаний и не лицензирован в мире. Напротив, отлаженные традиционные технологии изготовления инактивированных вакцин и их доказанная временем эффективность обусловливают реальные перспективы их практического применения в России и других европейских странах. analysis.background: Hantavirus fevers, including hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, are natural focal diseases with diverse clinical manifestations.
analysis.methods: The authors performed a literature review of existing hantavirus vaccines and ongoing development efforts, focusing on inactivated whole‑virion, subunit, VLP, viral vector, DNA, and mRNA platforms, and summarizing preclinical and phase I data.
analysis.results: Inactivated whole‑virion vaccines based on Hantaan and Seoul viruses show variable efficacy but reduce incidence in mass‑vaccinated regions and have low adverse event rates; several Russian inactivated vaccines have completed preclinical studies; DNA vaccines for Puumala and Hantaan have entered phase I trials, while no VLP, viral‑vector, or nucleic‑acid vaccine has completed full clinical cycles.
analysis.contribution: The review highlights the need for a Russian and European HFRS vaccine, underscores the practical prospects of traditional inactivated vaccines, and identifies DNA vaccines as the closest to clinical implementation.
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus fevers, including HFRS and HPS, are natural focal diseases with diverse clinical manifestations. Methods: The authors reviewed existing hantavirus vaccines and development efforts, covering inactivated, subunit, VLP, viral vector, DNA, and mRNA platforms. Results: Inactivated whole‑virion vaccines reduce incidence with low adverse events; several Russian vaccines passed preclinical studies; DNA vaccines for Puumala and Hantaan are in phase I trials, while other platforms lack full clinical data. papers.title: Climate change as an amplifier of hantavirus risk in South Asia: a neglected nexus.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus is seroepidemiologically established in South Asian human populations and rodent reservoirs, with anti-hantavirus antibodies confirmed in occupational risk groups in India, an independent association with chronic kidney disease demonstrated in Sri Lanka, and co-infection with leptospirosis identified in more than one-fifth of hospitalized leptospirosis patients. Despite this, the intersection of these findings with the region's intensifying monsoon floods, rapid urbanization, and climate-driven rodent ecology remains entirely unexamined. This letter highlights the neglected climate-hantavirus nexus, identifies structural vulnerabilities that amplify transmission risk in South Asia, and calls for integrated flood-response surveillance and One Health coordination across the region.
papers.journal: Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene

papers.title: A noetic fractal-fractional dynamical formalism for history-dependent Seoul virus–Streptococcus pyogenes dual-pathogen interaction with physics-informed learning

source_records.title: A noetic fractal-fractional dynamical formalism for history-dependent Seoul virus–Streptococcus pyogenes dual-pathogen interaction with physics-informed learning

papers.full_text: A noetic fractal-fractional dynamical formalism for history-dependent Seoul virus–Streptococcus pyogenes dual-pathogen interaction with physics-informed learning Abstract Seoul virus is an important rodent-borne hantavirus that can cause serious illness in humans, while Streptococcus pyogenes is a clinically significant bacterial pathogen associated with a wide range of infections and severe complications. The interaction between these two infections is not well understood from a mathematical modeling perspective. In this work, we develop a fractal–fractional model to investigate the transmission and co-infection dynamics of Seoul virus and Streptococcus pyogenes. The model is described using the Atangana–Baleanu–Caputo fractal–fractional derivative so that the effects of memory and the nonuniform nature of disease transmission can be represented more realistically than in conventional integer-order models. Several mathematical properties of the proposed system are studied, including the existence and uniqueness of solutions and the behavior of the disease-free equilibrium. The basic reproduction number is obtained to identify the threshold conditions associated with the spread of the infections, and the Ulam–Hyers stability of the model is also examined. In addition to the theoretical analysis, a physics-informed neural network is constructed to approximate the solutions of the fractal–fractional system. The governing equations and initial conditions are incorporated into the neural-network training process, allowing the model structure to guide the numerical approximation. The simulations illustrate the influence of the fractional and fractal parameters on the evolution of the co-infection system and show that the PINN approach can reproduce the model dynamics with good accuracy. The findings suggest that combining fractal–fractional operators with physics-informed learning offers a useful way to study co-infectious disease systems in which memory, heterogeneity, and nonlinear interactions play an important role. analysis_zh.background: 首尔病毒 是一种重要的啮齿动物传播的 汉坦病毒,可导致人类严重疾病,Streptococcus pyogenes 是临床重要的细菌病原体;它们的相互作用在数学建模层面尚不清楚。
analysis_zh.methods: 构建了一个基于 Atangana–Baleanu–Caputo 导数的分形‐分数阶模型,以捕捉记忆效应和非均匀传播,并推导基本再生数、平衡分析及 Ulam‐Hyers 稳定性;随后构建了一个物理信息神经网络,将控制方程和初始条件纳入,以近似系统解。
analysis_zh.results: 模拟表明,分数阶和分形参数影响共感染动力学,且物理信息神经网络(PINN)能够较高精度再现模型动力学;基本再生数提供了传播的阈值条件。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究表明,将分形‐分数阶算子与物理信息学习相结合,为研究记忆效应、异质性和非线性交互重要的共感染疾病系统提供了有用的框架。
analysis_zh.limitations: 未提供实证数据或真实世界验证;仅给出抽象层面的信息,且未报告除模拟示例之外的定量结果。
