Mattar, et al. Hantavirus: From Seoul to the Andes — The Imperative Need to Include It in the Triage of Acute Febrile Syndrome. Infectio 2026; 30(3): 245-246 Keywords: Hantavirus, Acute Febrile Syndrome, Rattus norvegicus Palabras clave: Hantavirus, Síndrome febril agudo, Rattus norvegicus Hantaviruses belong to two worlds: the Old-World Seoul vi- rus (SV) and New World hantaviruses, such as the Sin Nombre virus (SNV) in North America and Andes virus in South Ameri- ca. SV is a cosmopolitan hantavirus that is transmitted by the common brown rat (Rattus norvegicus). The virus lives in urban rodents and travels on ships. It causes hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which has low lethality. New World hantaviruses, such as SNV and Andes virus, cause Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS), a condition with high lethality ranging between 30% and 40%. The transmission routes for both groups are similar, primarily occurring through contact with aerosolized rodent excretions and secretions1. The geography of zoonotic diseases is often marked by pro- found contrast. In the fabric of global health, few pathogens exemplify this as starkly as hantavirus. In the Old World, SV adapted to synanthropic rodents (Rattus rattus, Rattus nor- vegicus, and Mus musculus), which in turn adapted to urban environments enriched with human food waste. SV is trans- mitted in metropolitan settings with moderate lethality ra- tes, although it may be underdiagnosed or misdiagnosed as other conditions, such as leptospirosis, particularly in Latin America, where cases are rarely reported2. In contrast, the na- rrative of the New World SNV changes completely. * Autor para correspondencia: Correo electrónico: smattar@correo.unicordoba.edu.co; mattarsalim@gmail.com In the Americas, hantaviruses emerge from wild ecosystems with high virulence and present clinically as HCPS. The vec- tors of these viruses are wild sigmodontine rodents (Oligory- zomys, Proechimys, Peromyscus, and Calomys) that feed on crops and local flora. However, evidence has demonstrated that SNV can infect multiple rodent species within geogra- phic regions experiencing human cases. This suggests that several rodent species may act as reservoirs and potential vectors for the transmission of H. longicornis to humans. Re- servoirs identified by SNV include Peromyscus boylii, Tamias minimus, and Mus musculus. The latter is ubiquitous in hou- seholds worldwide and is a well-known vector of the lym- phocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) and Leptospira (3). New World hantaviruses are widely distributed across North America and exhibit high diversity, including SNV, New York virus, and Black Creek Canal virus in the United States; Cho- clo virus in Panama; Maporal virus in Venezuela; Machupo virus in Bolivia; Laguna Negra virus in Paraguay; Sabiá virus in Brazil; and the recently prominent Andes virus (ANDV) in Argentina and Chile (Figure 1). Following the corridor of the formidable Andes mountain range, the virus moves steadily alongside its rodent hosts across the mountains, jungles, and valleys. ANDV has cha- llenged the classical virological paradigm that orthohanta- viruses are transmitted strictly via exposure to rodent secre- tions and excretions. ANDV possesses the unique capacity S. Mattar, et al 246 ASOCIACIÓN COLOMBIANA DE INFECTOLOGÍA REVISTA INFECTIO for interhuman airborne transmission, as documented during the M/V Hondius cruise ship outbreak in April 2026. A total of 13 confirmed cases and three fatalities were epidemio- logically linked to the vessel, forcing numerous passengers into mandatory quarantine across various countries. Never- theless, person-to-person transmission remains uncommon and is predominantly associated with household exposure, intimate contact, caregiving without adequate personal pro- tective equipment, and prolonged exposure to poorly venti- lated or overcrowded environments4,5. This epidemiological journey, spanning from the alleys of Seoul to the forested regions of South America, is not a ran- dom evolutionary artifact but rather a direct reflection of environmental boundaries repeatedly breached by human activity. Today, hantaviruses are no longer exotic rarities con- fined to the pages of tropical medicine textbooks. Accele- rating ecological degradation and expanding anthropogenic frontiers force host reservoirs out of mountain ranges and wild savannas into closer proximity to human populations. The evolving landscape of hantavirus infections poses a ma- jor diagnostic and therapeutic challenge for infectious disea- se specialists. The core challenge lies not merely in managing critical clinical outcomes but in establishing early clinical sus- picion. The eco-epidemiology of the disease demands the inclusion of hantavirus in diagnostic algorithms for acute undifferentiated febrile illness in emergency departments. Early symptoms overlap with numerous seasonal and tropical pathogens; thus, the differential diagnosis must encompass influenza, betacoronavirus infections, mycoplasmosis, Q fe- ver, leptospirosis, malaria, rickettsiosis, dengue, Zika, Chikun- gunya, Mayaro, and Oropouche5. Importantly, preceding the ANDV outbreak on the M/V Hon- dius in April 2026, the Ministry of Public Health of Argentina confirmed 12 hantavirus cases and two deaths in Salta Pro- vince between January and March. Most infections occurred in the Orán Department, involving 10 men and two women aged 20–50 years, while 50 additional suspected cases remai- ned under investigation across multiple departments6. Similarly, between February and July 2026, the Ministry of Health of Chile confirmed 41 hantavirus cases and 14 deaths (34% mortality rate). Cases were reported across 11 regions from Valparaíso to Aysén, with the highest incidence rates per 100,000 inhabitants recorded in Aysén (1.84), Los Ríos (0.96), and Ñuble (0.95). The causative agent was identified as ANDV, vectored by the long-tailed pygmy rice rat (Oligoryzomys lon- gicaudatus). In Venezuela, by late July 2026, three deaths pre- senting with symptoms compatible with HCPS were reported in Anzoátegui, alongside two unexplained deaths among phy- sicians in Barinas; these cases remain unconfirmed7. Hantavirus outbreaks in Argentina, Chile, and the M/V Hon- dius cruise ship in 2026 highlight the need to revise epide- miological perspectives and clinical approaches to acute un- differentiated febrile illness in Latin America. The cruise ship outbreak remains one of the most significant events invol- ving ANDV, the only known hantavirus capable of interhu- man transmission. The outbreak was officially declared over, with no active transmission detected8. This eco-epidemiological and clinical challenge requires the expansion of diagnostic algorithms. The primary danger of hantavirus lies in its chameleon-like presentation during the early stages. Following anthropogenic ecosystem disruption and subsequent reservoir exposure5, patients enter a prodro- mal phase that closely mimics common tropical infections or viral respiratory illnesses, such as COVID-19. During the first 3 to 5 days, symptoms manifest as an acute undifferentiated febrile syndrome characterized by sudden high fever (>39°C), severe myalgias (particularly involving the back and lower ex- tremities), headache, chills, diaphoresis, and gastrointestinal distress, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain1,2. Increased vascular permeability driven by endothelial dysfunction is the hallmark feature of HCPS, driven by ele- vated viral loads and dysregulated inflammatory mediators, such as tumor necrosis factor, interleukin-6, and interferon- gamma. During this critical window, hantavirus infection is frequently misdiagnosed as dengue, influenza, leptospirosis, or COVID-19. In the case of ANDV, the transition to full HCPS Figure 1. Global distribution of the most important hantaviruses. SNV (Sin Nombre virus). Hantavirus: From Seoul to the Andes — The Imperative Need to Include It in the Triage of Acute Febrile Syndrome 247 occurs abruptly within hours, triggering a cytokine storm that leads to massive capillary leakage, non-cardiogenic pulmo- nary edema, and cardiogenic shock with high mortality ra- tes2,4. In most instances, establishing a diagnosis once frank respiratory failure develops is too late. This manuscript highlights an urgent priority for emergency triage: hantavirus must not remain a late diagnosis of exclu- sion but rather an active consideration in the systematic eva- luation of acute febrile syndromes and atypical pneumonias. Clinical suspicion should not be restricted to unexplained respiratory failure. We formally propose the integration of hantavirus into differential diagnostic protocols for patients reporting exposure to rural or wild environments within the preceding 4 weeks1. In countries such as Colombia, where endemic zones remain poorly defined, clinicians must rely on subtle early laboratory clues. The combination of thrombo- cytopenia, hemoconcentration, and circulating immunoblasts (atypical lymphocytes) on peripheral blood smears provides a cost-effective triad of suspicion prior to the appearance of bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiography1-5. When routine respiratory panels yield negative results in pa- tients with rapidly progressive pneumonia or in those pre- senting with febrile syndromes accompanied by early hema- tologic abnormalities, ordering IgM/IgG serology or RT-PCR for hantavirus should be protocolized9. IgM antibodies are detectable in nearly 100% of patients during the prodromal phase and persist for 2–3 months. Concurrently, IgG levels rise rapidly and appear to persist for years, although it re- mains uncertain whether these antibodies confer long-term neutralizing protection9. This rapid serological response at clinical onset makes ELISA the diagnostic tool of choice in emergency settings, outperforming RT-PCR in later stages, as the viral load declines rapidly after the first week of illness5. Furthermore, the unique capacity of ANDV for person-to- person transmission5 elevates early diagnosis from a clinical necessity to an urgent priority for hospital biosecurity and public health. Suspecting hantavirus infection at first contact in emergency departments is not an overreaction; it repre- sents the single opportunity to alter a potentially fatal course. In Colombia, the potential circulation of ANDV remains unk- nown, necessitating expanded seroprevalence and ecological reservoir research. Serologically, ANDV displays cross-reacti- vity with other New World hantaviruses, particularly SNV. We hypothesized that native Colombian hantaviruses may mani- fest with less aggressive clinical presentations than ANDV or SNV. This aligns with the findings of five patients diagnosed with IgM seroconversion in Córdoba and Meta10,11, presen- ting clinical features similar to those documented for Choclo virus in Panama12. To date, molecular detection in Colombia has been limited to a short genomic segment of the Neco- clí virus identified in wild rodents (Zygodontomys cherriei), although its human pathogenicity remains uncharacterized13. The geographic span of hantaviruses from North America to Patagonia underscores the fragility of ecological boundaries, which are dynamic interfaces that elevate global disease risk. Addressing this challenge requires a paradigm shift in clinical practices. Infectious disease and emergency medicine can no longer operate in isolation from environmental changes; the clinician’s diagnostic approach must be aligned with local te- rritorial ecology and epidemiology5,14. Systematically incorporating hantavirus into emergency tria- ge for acute febrile illness and atypical pneumonia is not an abstract taxonomical exercise but an essential clinical and public health imperative. In Colombia, substantial knowledge gaps remain regarding rodent-borne pathogens, particularly hantaviruses and Arenaviruses. Early clinical suspicion rema- ins the most effective tool in emergency medicine. Learning to recognize subtle epidemiological and hematological sig- nals in the early stages provides the only realistic window for intervention before fatal complications arise, a race against time in which early detection represents a major victory for preventive medicine. papers.title: Network-Guided Drug Repurposing for Hantaan Virus Infection in Endothelial Cells: Pathway Analysis, Target Identification, and Mechanistic ODE Simulations
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, which are together the cause of more than 200,000 human cases every year. However, no specific antiviral therapy is approved. Here, we develop a three-stage computational framework for systematic drug repurposing. Transcriptome-wide analysis of hantavirus-infected human endothelial cells showed a response dominated by interferon pathways. A STRING protein–protein interaction network and a composite network centrality score identified 15 hub genes, including ISG15, IRF1, CXCL10, STAT1, and DDX58. Druggability and literature analysis of these hubs provided 12 repurposing candidates across four priority tiers. An ordinary differential equation (ODE) model of type I interferon signalling then evaluated eight drug perturbations. Early IFN-β achieved the fastest viral clearance (3.5 days) with reduced CXCL10 output. Early JAK inhibition delayed clearance (4.9 days) and increased IRF1-driven CXCL10. Our simulation showed that IFN-β combined with an anti-CXCL10 monoclonal antibody produced the best balance between antiviral effect and CXCL10 output. A structural sensitivity analysis showed the antiviral predictions to hold under an alternative network topology, while the chemokine predictions depended on it. This computational pipeline prioritises candidate therapies and phase-specific combinations for preclinical hantavirus studies.

analysis_zh.methods: 作者构建了一个三阶段计算框架:对 汉坦病毒 感染的人类内皮细胞进行全转录组分析,利用 STRING 蛋白‐蛋白相互作用网络的中心性识别 15 个枢纽基因,进行药物可及性和文献筛选以挑选 12 个再利用候选药物,并建立 I 型干扰素信号的常微分方程模型评估 8 种药物扰动。
analysis_zh.results: 模拟结果显示,早期 IFN‐β 可实现最快的病毒清除(3.5 天),伴随 CXCL10 降低;早期 JAK 抑制延迟清除(4.9 天)并导致 CXCL10 增高;IFN‐β 与抗 CXCL10 单克隆抗体联合使用获得最佳的抗病毒‐趋化因子平衡;敏感性分析表明,抗病毒预测对网络变化具有鲁棒性,而趋化因子预测则依赖于网络拓扑。

analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要,未报告详细的实验验证和完整的方法学细节。

papers.title: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome: an emerging fatal zoonotic infection.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome is a potentially fatal respiratory zoonotic infection caused by New World hantaviruses, and it is acquired mostly via inhaling aerosolized excreta from infected rodents. Over the past 30 years, HCPS has expanded beyond its initial foci, and recent events suggest a potential for spread beyond traditionally endemic regions. The disease rapidly progresses from a vague prodrome to acute cardiopulmonary failure with a high fatality rate despite optimum supportive treatment. Pathophysiology involves endothelial failure, increased vascular permeability, acute thrombocytopenia and excessive immunological responses resulting in capillary leak syndrome and cardiogenic shock. It is still hard to clinically suspect early since the prodromal symptoms are vague and mirror common viral infections and respiratory disorders. Diagnostic confirmation needs serological testing or genetic approaches, which are typically unavailable in resource-limited endemic situations, leading to considerable diagnostic delays. Management is generally supportive, with early ICU admission, judicious hydration management, mechanical breathing and cardiopulmonary support including extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in refractory patients. The recent multi-country Andes virus epidemic on a cruise ship in May 2026 highlights the potential for fast worldwide transmission of HCPS outside of usual endemic settings. This review summarizes the current information on the epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic techniques, and treatment options for HCPS. We also highlight the pressing need for improved global surveillance, rapid point-of-care diagnostics, global awareness among health care workers, and ongoing development of preventive vaccines and effective antiviral therapies to address this significant public health threat.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒心肺综合征:一种新出现的致命人畜共患感染。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒心肺综合征(HCPS)是一种潜在致命的呼吸道人畜共患病,由新世界 汉坦病毒es 引起,主要通过吸入啮齿动物排泄物的气溶胶获得。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述涉及流行病学、病理生理学、临床表现、诊断方法和治疗,重点强调内皮功能衰竭、毛细血管渗漏以及支持性 ICU 护理。
analysis_zh.current_state: 汉坦病毒心肺综合征(HCPS)在出现模糊的前驱期后迅速进展为急性心肺衰竭,即使在最佳支持治疗下,死亡率仍然很高。
analysis_zh.gaps: 早期临床怀疑较为困难,因为前驱症状缺乏特异性,且类似于常见的病毒或呼吸道疾病。
analysis_zh.future_research: 作者强调需要加强全球监测、快速的现场诊断、提升临床医生的警觉性,以及研发预防性疫苗和有效的抗病毒药物。

papers.title: Hantavirus infection in Ukraine and the world: comparative analysis of the incidence dynamics of servicemen and civilians in peacetime and wartime
papers.abstract: Introduction. Every year, about 200 thousand cases of hantavirus infection are detected at the global level, a significant number of which have a course in the form of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Asia and Europe. The rapid course of the disease, the high mortality rate of its individual strains, which are mainly found in the Western Hemisphere, the lack of etiotropic pharmacotherapy and vaccination opportunities, as well as the characteristic features of the route of transmission of hantavirus disease (infection in the predominant most cases occurs as a result of contact with rodent body fluids), indicate that hantavirus infection remains a significant challenge to the health care system, which, nevertheless, is sporadic. Purpose. To highlight the quantitative indicators of the incidence of hantavirus infection in Ukraine among servicemen and civilians from 2014 until now in peacetime and wartime and compare them with the dynamics of incidence in specific countries and on different continents of the world. Materials and methods. In the course of forming the results of the study, the authors resorted to the bibliographic method, the method of information synthesis, comparison and generalization. The analysis of scientific literature on the subject of the work took place in the scientometric databases Scopus, PubMed, Google Scholar for the period from 2014 to the present. The value of the reliability of the approximation of the trend in the incidence of hantavirus infection among servicemen stationed in the Sumy region for the period from May to July 2025 inclusive was calculated, relative visualization was given without specifying absolute numbers, a graph of the specified trend was built, its line and equation were displayed. Results. During 2021-2026, it is worth noting the significant spatio-temporal diversity of hantavirus incidence, which is caused by the interrelated cumulative impact of the climatic features of a particular region, the transformation of ecosystems and the level of urbanization associated with the activities of the human species. In the context of the aggregate incidence of hantavirus disease among servicemen and civilians of Ukraine for the first quarter of 2026, it should be noted that a total of 63 cases of this disease were detected, which may indicate the continuation of a rapid trend and an exponential increase in the number of registered cases for the above-mentioned nosology in 2026 (as of March 2026). Conclusion. The analysis of the incidence of hantavirus infection in Ukraine from 2014 to 2026 indicates a unique epidemiological transition: from a long period of latent endemicity with sporadic case registration to a sudden epidemic outbreak in 2025-2026. In 2025, as a result of hostilities and the associated cascade of environmental factors, an increase in the incidence of this disease among the civilian population was registered in Ukraine, namely, 436 cases, of which 428 cases (which is 98.16% for the specified period) were detected in the Sumy region, which provoked an increase in the incidence among the servicemen of the Armed Forces of Ukraine stationed in the specified region, in particular, from May to July 2025 inclusive. The obtained trend of incidence dynamics for the specified period is highly reliable, since its value of the reliability of the approximation R2 is 0.8621 and this value is in the range from 0.8 to 1.0.

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒 在全球范围内(尤其是亚洲和欧洲)导致 肾综合征出血热,因其病程迅速、死亡率高且缺乏特异性治疗或疫苗,仍是重大健康挑战。
analysis_zh.methods: 本研究采用文献计量方法,综合并比较 Scopus、PubMed 和 Google Scholar(2014 至今)的数据;对 Sumy 区军人(2025 年 5‐7 月)的发病趋势进行建模,可靠性系数 R2=0.8621。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究提供了乌克兰平时与战时军人和平民之间 汉坦病毒 发病动态的比较分析,突出时空多样性和环境驱动因素。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告。

papers.title: Transmission potential of Andes virus.
papers.abstract: We read with interest the Comment published in The Lancet Microbe by Jason R Andrews and Isaac I Bogoch,1 who highlighted that the largest Andes virus outbreaks are driven by rare superspreading events, whereas most outbreaks undergo rapid stochastic extinction. This finding implies that widespread transmission is unlikely. We agree and note that the basic reproduction number, R0, might be lower than they estimated, further strengthening this conclusion.

Is human-to-human transmission of Andes virus truly established? Lessons from the Hondius Cruise Ship experience. Infect Dis Clin Microbiol. 2026;8(5):442–5. DOI: 10.36519/idcm.2026.1246 Is Human-to-Human Transmission of Andes Virus Truly Established? Lessons from the Hondius Cruise Ship Experience This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License. Deniz Güllü1,2 , Defne Yigci1 , Önder Ergönül2,3 1 Koç University School of Medicine, İstanbul, Türkiye 2 Koç University İşBank Center for Infectious Diseases (KUISCID), İstanbul, Türkiye 3 Department of Infectious Diseases and Clinical Microbiology, Koç University School of Medicine, İstanbul, Türkiye TO THE EDITOR, T he recent cluster of Andes virus (ANDV) infection associated with the MV Hon- dius adventure cruise ship has sparked global concern about the virus's pan- demic potential (1). Cruise ships may provide favorable conditions for examining human-to-human transmission due to prolonged close contact. We reviewed the exist- ing literature to shed light on the subject. Most hantaviruses are considered strictly zoonotic pathogens. The primary route of trans- mission is through the inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta or contaminated environ- mental particles. However, reports from South America have suggested that ANDV may occasionally spread between humans under specific conditions. Initial reports emerged from family clusters in southern Argentina and Chile during the 1990s (2–4) (Figure 1). Investigators identified infections occurring after prolonged close exposure to symptom- atic patients (3). In later years, epidemiologic and molecular studies described additional clusters involving household members, sexual partners, and healthcare workers (5,6). A prospective study from Chile suggested that sexual partners and close household con- tacts had substantially higher infection risk than non-intimate contacts (7). Human-to-Human Transmission of Andes Virus Güllü D et al. 443 The strongest evidence of human-to-human trans- mission came from the 2018–2019 Epuyén out- break in Argentina. Martínez et al. (8) described 34 confirmed cases and proposed a “super-spreading” event during crowded gatherings. Using epidemi- ological reconstruction and genomic sequencing methods, researchers suggested that secondary transmission chains occurred following a single spillover. The authors estimated a median repro- ductive number of 2.12 before implementation of isolation and quarantine measures, decreasing to 0.96 afterward (8). However, reproduction numbers obtained from relatively small and highly clustered outbreaks are sensitive to assumptions about transmission chains, timing of exposure, and case attribution. During the Epuyén outbreak, transmis- sion appeared disproportionately associated with a limited number of individuals classified as “super- spreaders”. This suggests that social behavior and exposure intensity may have contributed to out- break dynamics. Accordingly, the estimated repro- ductive number may reflect the characteristics of the outbreak rather than the intrinsic transmis- sibility of ANDV itself. It is uncertain whether the reproduction number would be informative in the recent cruise ship-associated cluster. Furthermore, Figure 1. Timeline of reported Andes virus outbreaks and factors associated with human-to-human transmission. Infect Dis Clin Microbiol 2026; 8(5): 442–5 This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License. 444 such a high reproduction number has not been reported in other ANDV outbreaks. According to the authors, the human-to-human transmission win- dow of the virus was approximately one day, which may limit opportunities for transmission. Despite the available evidence suggesting potential human-to-human transmission, important epide- miologic and methodological limitations remain. In endemic rural areas, particularly among socially connected individuals living in close geographical proximity, shared environmental rodent exposure cannot always be ruled out. Recall bias, incomplete contact histories, and uncertainty regarding the pre- cise timing of infectivity challenge retrospective out- break analyses. The long incubation period of ANDV, which can extend up to 8 weeks, complicates the accurate reconstruction of exposure timelines and transmission chains. Genomic similarity between isolates may support an epidemiological link, but it does not independently prove direct human-to-hu- man transmission, since closely related viral strains can circulate within the same endemic region. Broader epidemiologic evidence also remains inconsistent. A systematic review by Toledo et al. (9) concluded that comparative studies did not provide strong evidence supporting widespread human- to-human transmission of hantaviruses, although limited transmission could not be excluded. Several seroepidemiologic studies evaluating healthcare workers and exposed household contacts similarly failed to demonstrate markedly increased seropos- itivity compared with the general population (2,7). In addition, no sustained community outbreaks resembling influenza-like respiratory spread have been documented despite decades of hantavirus surveillance in endemic regions. Therefore, the MV Hondius cluster offers a signifi- cant opportunity to re-evaluate these questions. Cruise ships represent theoretically favorable set- tings for transmission because of prolonged close contact, shared dining areas, confined social envi- ronments, and repeated interaction among passen- gers and crew members. The outbreak extended from symptom onset in the first probable case on April 2, 2026, to the last confirmed case on May 31, 2026, and was announced as over on July 2, 2026 (1). Since the incubation period of ANDV may extend to 8 weeks, this temporal pattern is com- patible with one or more transmission generations. Nonetheless, only 13 cases were identified among 147 passengers and crew members (1). The World Health Organization (WHO) initially estimated the effective reproduction number to be approximately 0.7 (10), consistent with limited transmission. Fol- lowing completion of the recommended 42-day follow-up, 317 high-risk and 336 low-risk contacts were monitored without identification of additional secondary cases. If ANDV consistently possessed highly efficient human-to-human transmissibility, broader dissemination might reasonably have been expected in such conditions. Instead, the restricted extent of spread may suggest that transmission requires highly specific epidemiologic circum- stances or intense close exposure rather than rou- tine casual interaction. Interpretation of the cruise-associated cluster remains complex. Some of the passengers report- edly participated in outdoor excursions and hiking activities in South America before symptom onset, introducing the possibility of rodent-associated environmental exposure before embarkation (11). Preliminary genomic analysis identified a single monophyletic viral lineage among cases from dif- ferent countries. This pattern is compatible with a common zoonotic introduction followed by sub- sequent spread (12). Together with the epidemio- logic investigation, these findings support limited human-to-human transmission aboard the vessel. Still, genomic data alone cannot resolve individual transmission chains or fully exclude alternative epidemiological scenarios. The outbreak additionally highlights important operational challenges relevant to future emerg- ing infections. The prolonged incubation period of ANDV complicates identification of index exposures and secondary cases. Rapid point-of- care diagnostic tests suitable for deployment in closed environments such as cruise ships remain unavailable. Moreover, current international sur- veillance systems are not optimized for rapid, coordinated investigation of uncommon zoonotic outbreaks involving multiple countries and mobile populations. The MV Hondius cluster adds valuable real-world experience to the limited literature regarding possi- ble human-to-human transmission of ANDV. After screening more than 600 people, available evidence does not support characterization of ANDV as a readily transmissible pandemic-prone respiratory virus. While some experts took a cautious approach to this outbreak at the beginning, the available evi- dence suggests that self-quarantine measures may be sufficient.

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) is primarily a zoonotic hantavirus, but reports from South America have suggested occasional human‑to‑human (H2H) spread, raising concern about its pandemic potential, especially after a recent cluster on the MV Hondius cruise ship.
analysis.methods: The authors performed a literature review of existing reports and studies on ANDV transmission.
analysis.results: The strongest H2H evidence comes from the 2018‑2019 Epuyén outbreak in Argentina, with 34 confirmed cases and an estimated median reproductive number of 2.12 before isolation measures, dropping to 0.96 afterward; however, the authors note that such estimates may reflect outbreak‑specific factors and may not apply to the cruise‑ship cluster.
analysis.contribution: The commentary synthesizes current evidence on ANDV H2H transmission, highlighting the cruise‑ship setting as a useful model for studying transmission dynamics and informing surveillance and control strategies.
analysis.limitations: The analysis is limited to published reports, subject to recall bias, incomplete contact histories, and difficulty excluding shared rodent exposure; thus, conclusions are based on indirect evidence rather than new primary data.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus is mainly zoonotic, but possible human‑to‑human spread has been reported, prompting concern after a cruise‑ship cluster. Methods: The authors reviewed the literature on ANDV transmission. Results: The Epuyén outbreak showed 34 cases with a median reproductive number of 2.12 pre‑isolation and 0.96 post‑isolation, but these figures may reflect specific outbreak conditions and not the cruise scenario. Contribution: This commentary consolidates evidence on ANDV H2H transmission and underscores cruise ships as valuable settings for surveillance and response planning. Limitations: Reliance on existing reports introduces recall bias, incomplete contacts, and uncertainty about rodent exposure, and no new primary data were generated.

papers.title: Plasma Exchange for Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome: A Mechanistic Case for an Untested Intervention.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) carries a case fatality rate of 35%-40% and has no approved pharmacologic treatment. Its pathophysiology is rooted in the plasma compartment: cytokines, viral antigens, immune complexes, and platelet-binding glycoproteins circulate as drivers of immunopathologic endothelial injury, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and cardiogenic depression. Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) achieves bulk clearance of plasma-borne mediators and is established by the American Society for Apheresis (ASFA) for numerous indications that share an analogous mechanistic rationale. This commentary argues that the immunopathology of HPS maps onto the therapeutic targets of TPE, that any intervention would need to be timed to the early cardiopulmonary phase, and that the coagulopathic dimension of the disease provides a mechanistic argument for incorporating plasma into the replacement strategy. We deliberately situate this rationale against the uneven record of TPE in diseases of comparable pathophysiology, in which the intervention has been effective in some settings and without demonstrable benefit in others. The recent Andes virus outbreak aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, which produced a multinational cluster of severe cardiopulmonary cases, prompted us, as transfusion medicine and apheresis physicians, to articulate this hypothesis. We emphasize that these arguments are mechanistic and hypothesis-generating rather than evidence-based: no clinical data yet support TPE in HPS, and systematic outcome reporting, ideally through a multicenter case series, would be required before any conclusion about efficacy could be drawn.

papers.full_text: Plasma Exchange for Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome: A Mechanistic Case for an Untested Intervention ABSTRACT Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) carries a case fatality rate of 35%–40% and has no approved pharmacologic treatment. Its pathophysiology is rooted in the plasma compartment: cytokines, viral antigens, immune complexes, and platelet‐binding glycoproteins circulate as drivers of immunopathologic endothelial injury, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and cardiogenic depression. Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) achieves bulk clearance of plasma‐borne mediators and is established by the American Society for Apheresis (ASFA) for numerous indications that share an analogous mechanistic rationale. This commentary argues that the immunopathology of HPS maps onto the therapeutic targets of TPE, that any intervention would need to be timed to the early cardiopulmonary phase, and that the coagulopathic dimension of the disease provides a mechanistic argument for incorporating plasma into the replacement strategy. We deliberately situate this rationale against the uneven record of TPE in diseases of comparable pathophysiology, in which the intervention has been effective in some settings and without demonstrable benefit in others. The recent Andes virus outbreak aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, which produced a multinational cluster of severe cardiopulmonary cases, prompted us, as transfusion medicine and apheresis physicians, to articulate this hypothesis. We emphasize that these arguments are mechanistic and hypothesis‐generating rather than evidence‐based: no clinical data yet support TPE in HPS, and systematic outcome reporting, ideally through a multicenter case series, would be required before any conclusion about efficacy could be drawn. Introduction Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), caused primarily by Sin Nombre virus in North America and Andes virus in South America, remains one of the most lethal respiratory infections encountered in the Western Hemisphere. Since its identification following the 1993 Four Corners outbreak, HPS has been characterized by a case fatality rate approaching 35%–40%, a figure that has not materially improved in three decades despite advances in critical care. No antiviral agent has demonstrated efficacy in controlled trials. Ribavirin, the most extensively studied candidate, failed to reduce mortality in a prospective randomized trial and is not recommended for treatment of established HPS. Management remains entirely supportive: mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure, vasopressors for cardiogenic and distributive shock, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) as a rescue strategy in refractory cases . The persistent gap between the severity of this disease and the poverty of its treatment options invites reexamination of established extracorporeal therapies. Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE), a procedure central to transfusion medicine practice and codified in the American Society for Apheresis (ASFA) guidelines for more than 40 indications, has never been formally evaluated or published as a treatment for HPS. This commentary argues that the immunopathology of HPS maps onto the mechanistic rationale for TPE, that the plasma compartment represents a plausible site of actionable pathology, and that the replacement fluid strategy in this context deserves specific attention from a transfusion medicine perspective. We advance these points as a hypothesis to be tested rather than as a recommendation for immediate practice. Two considerations prompted this commentary. The first is mechanistic and is developed below. The second is circumstantial. The 2026 outbreak of Andes virus infection aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, which generated a multinational cluster of hantavirus cardiopulmonary cases with a case fatality ratio within the range historically reported for the disease, returned clinical and public health attention to a syndrome whose therapeutic options have remained essentially static for three decades. We write as transfusion medicine and apheresis physicians rather than as clinicians with first‐hand experience managing HPS, and we are deliberately explicit about that vantage point. Our aim is to frame a mechanistically coherent hypothesis from the perspective of the extracorporeal therapies we practice, so that centers that do encounter these patients, whether in sporadic cases or in the next cluster, are positioned to evaluate and report outcomes systematically. Pathophysiology: The Plasma Compartment as Battlefield Understanding why TPE is mechanistically rational for HPS requires understanding why HPS kills (Figure 1). Hantaviruses infect pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells without inducing direct cytopathic effect. Infected endothelial cells remain architecturally intact; it is the immune response mounted against viral antigens displayed on their surface that destroys the vascular barrier. Cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes, recruited in disproportionate numbers, drive immunopathologic endothelial injury through perforin and granzyme‐mediated mechanisms. The result is not pneumonia in the conventional sense but a diffuse increase in pulmonary vascular permeability, causing protein‐rich fluid to flood the alveolar compartment. The clinical syndrome that follows, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema progressing to refractory hypoxemia within 24–48 h of the cardiopulmonary phase onset, reflects this mechanism precisely. Conceptual rationale for plasma‐directed extracorporeal therapy in hantavirus pulmonary syndrome. TPE and cytokine‐directed extracorporeal therapies are presented as theoretical, hypothesis‐generating approaches; clinical efficacy remains unproven. The cytokine milieu in HPS is the proximate driver of this process. Circulating levels of tumor necrosis factor‐alpha (TNF‐alpha), interleukin‐6 (IL‐6), interleukin‐10 (IL‐10), and interferon‐gamma are markedly elevated in patients with severe disease, correlating with clinical deterioration. These mediators perpetuate endothelial activation, upregulate adhesion molecule expression, and amplify capillary leak beyond the initial viral trigger. Simultaneously, thrombocytopenia, universally observed in HPS, reflects platelet consumption, impaired thrombopoiesis, and direct binding of hantavirus glycoproteins to platelet integrin alpha‐IIb‐beta‐3. Viral antigens and immune complexes circulate during the acute phase, potentially sustaining toll‐like receptor and innate immune activation even as viremia begins to clear. The myocardial depression characteristic of HPS adds a cardiogenic component to what is otherwise a distributive and permeability‐driven shock syndrome. Depressed left ventricular ejection fraction in the acute phase is well described and reflects the effects of circulating mediators on myocardial contractility rather than ischemia or direct viral invasion. This low cardiac output state, superimposed on alveolar flooding from capillary leak, produces the particularly lethal hemodynamic phenotype that distinguishes HPS from other viral pneumonias and has prompted the preferred designation hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). The central observation for the transfusion medicine audience is this: the pathogenic burden in HPS is not primarily cellular or structural. It is humoral. Cytokines, viral antigens, immune complexes, activated complement fragments, and dysfunctional platelet‐binding viral glycoproteins all circulate in plasma. The plasma compartment is both the propagation medium and the therapeutic target. Mechanistic Rationale for Therapeutic Plasma Exchange TPE removes one to one and a half plasma volumes per session, clearing approximately 63%–78% of any given plasma constituent in a single procedure. In diseases characterized by pathogenic circulating mediators, this degree of bulk clearance exceeds what pharmacologic suppression or renal replacement therapy can achieve on a comparable timescale. The ASFA guidelines assign Category I or II designations to disorders spanning autoimmune, hematologic, and neurologic disease on exactly this basis. Applied to HPS, TPE would be expected to achieve several mechanistic objectives simultaneously. Cytokine clearance is the most immediate rationale. TNF‐alpha, IL‐6, and interferon‐gamma are predominantly plasma‐borne mediators in the molecular weight range of 17 to 26 kDa, well within the clearance profile of centrifugal plasma separation. A single 1.0 plasma volume exchange reduces circulating cytokine levels by approximately 50 to 65% before endogenous resynthesis begins. In a disease where the severity and duration of the cytokine storm directly predict mortality, even a transient reduction in circulating mediator burden could plausibly interrupt the immunopathologic cascade before irreversible lung injury is fully established. This therapeutic window, corresponding roughly to Days 4–8 of illness when the cardiopulmonary phase begins, is when any intervention would need to be timed. Viral antigen and immune complex removal represents a distinct and complementary rationale. Hantavirus nucleocapsid antigen and glycoprotein fragments circulate during the acute viremic phase, potentially sustaining innate immune activation through pattern recognition receptor engagement. Immune complexes formed between viral antigens and early antibody responses can deposit in vascular beds and amplify complement‐mediated endothelial injury. TPE removes both the antigen burden and the complexes formed against it, reducing the substrate for ongoing complement activation. Restoration of ADAMTS13 and endothelial‐protective proteins is a mechanism that has received insufficient attention in the emerging infection literature but is relevant here. Severe inflammatory states consume ADAMTS13, the von Willebrand factor‐cleaving protease whose deficiency underlies thrombotic microangiopathy. Whether HPS is accompanied by clinically significant ADAMTS13 depletion has not been formally studied, but the consumptive coagulopathy and platelet dysfunction observed in the disease create a phenotype that could benefit from restoration of this and other regulatory plasma proteins. Replacement Fluid Strategy: A Transfusion Medicine Perspective The choice of replacement fluid in TPE for HPS deserves specific consideration and distinguishes this hypothetical indication from the majority of ASFA‐guided diseases in which albumin alone suffices. In most established indications, albumin replacement is preferred because it avoids the infectious and allergic risks associated with plasma products and adequately restores oncotic pressure. In HPS, however, the coagulopathic dimension of the disease argues for a different calculus. Patients in the cardiopulmonary phase of HPS frequently exhibit prolonged prothrombin times, elevated fibrin degradation products, and reduced fibrinogen, reflecting a consumptive coagulopathic process superimposed on severe thrombocytopenia. In this setting, albumin‐only replacement across serial exchanges would be expected to accelerate depletion of residual coagulation factors by dilution, potentially worsening an already compromised hemostatic capacity. This concern provides a mechanistic argument for using plasma for all or a substantial portion of the exchange volume in HPS. We stress, however, that this remains a mechanistic argument and not an evidence‐based one: albumin replacement has not been shown to be ineffective or harmful in HPS, no comparative data exist, and the choice of replacement fluid in any individual patient must weigh the theoretical hemostatic benefit of plasma against its infectious, allergic, and TRALI‐associated risks. Beyond coagulation factor repletion, plasma provides alpha‐2‐macroglobulin (a broad‐spectrum protease inhibitor and cytokine carrier), protein C and antithrombin (anti‐inflammatory and anticoagulant mediators consumed during critical illness), and endothelial‐protective proteins that are stripped away by the inflammatory milieu. This argument parallels the rationale for plasma replacement in TPE for thrombotic microangiopathy, where ADAMTS13 repletion is the explicit therapeutic goal. In HPS, the goal would be broader, but the logic is analogous: replace what the disease process has consumed while simultaneously removing what it has generated in excess. The strength of this analogy, however, should not be overstated in the absence of any HPS‐specific data. Practical considerations regarding ABO compatibility and the risk of transfusion‐related acute lung injury (TRALI) in a patient with already‐compromised pulmonary reserve require careful attention and close coordination between the apheresis service and the intensive care unit. Because the residual risk of transfusion‐transmitted viral infection from modern plasma products is already very low, the incremental safety benefit of pathogen‐reduced plasma in this context is modest; where such products are available, however, they may offer an additional margin of safety that is reasonable to prefer given the setting of active viral infection. The volume dynamics of a 1.0–1.5 plasma volume exchange in a hemodynamically unstable patient with diminished cardiac reserve mandate continuous hemodynamic monitoring throughout the procedure and may require vasopressor support during the exchange itself. Alternative Extracorporeal Strategies: Cytokine Adsorption and Hemofiltration TPE is not the only extracorporeal option capable of lowering the circulating mediator burden in HPS, and any argument for it must account for the alternatives. Selective cytokine adsorption columns, such as those incorporating porous polymer beads, and high‐volume hemofiltration both reduce plasma cytokine concentrations and have been described in cytokine‐driven critical illness, including a reported case of hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome treated with high‐volume hemofiltration. These modalities carry real advantages in the coagulopathic HPS patient: they do not require large volumes of plasma, they avoid the transfusion exposure and TRALI risk inherent to plasma replacement, and adsorption can often be integrated into an existing continuous renal replacement circuit. Their principal limitation relative to TPE is that they are subtractive only. Adsorption and hemofiltration remove cytokines within a defined size range but do not efficiently clear larger immune complexes and do not replete the regulatory and hemostatic plasma proteins that the disease consumes. TPE is distinctive precisely because it couples broad removal with simultaneous restoration of plasma composition, the feature most relevant to the consumptive coagulopathy of HPS. We do not regard these approaches as mutually exclusive; in a given patient, adsorption, hemofiltration, and TPE could prove complementary, and the relative merits of each remain entirely untested in this disease. Precedent and Positioning TPE has not been used for HPS in any published report, but extracorporeal cytokine removal has. High‐volume continuous hemofiltration (HVHF) was applied to a patient with HCPS and refractory cardiogenic shock in a 2016 Chilean case report, with hemodynamic improvement within hours of initiation. The authors attributed the benefit specifically to cytokine clearance across the hemofilter membrane. If cytokine removal via CRRT can influence the HPS shock state, the case for TPE, which achieves cytokine clearance with greater efficiency per unit time and simultaneously restores plasma protein composition, is at least worth examining. A single case report, however, cannot establish efficacy for either modality. Convalescent plasma has also been examined in the HPS context, with a small interventional study demonstrating a borderline‐significant reduction in case fatality rate when administered early in the viremic phase. Convalescent plasma and TPE are mechanistically distinct: the former provides neutralizing antibodies against viral antigens, the latter removes pathogenic circulating mediators. They could in principle be complementary in a sequential protocol, with TPE addressing the immunopathologic phase and convalescent plasma targeting viremia in the days preceding it. The analogy to antibody replacement following TPE in myasthenia gravis is imperfect but instructive. More broadly, TPE has been applied to cytokine‐storm syndromes of diverse etiology including hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, macrophage activation syndrome, and severe COVID‐19, where the pathophysiology shares important features with HPS: immunopathologic endothelial injury, consumptive coagulopathy, and cytokine‐driven organ failure. The mechanistic parallels support extrapolation of the TPE rationale to HPS, while acknowledging that the viral trigger and the specific immune effector populations differ. This mechanistic optimism must be tempered by the uneven record of TPE across diseases whose pathophysiology superficially resembles that of HPS, because plausibility has repeatedly failed to predict benefit. On the favorable side, TPE is unambiguously life‐saving in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, and it has produced apparent benefit in selected reports of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, macrophage activation syndrome, and catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome, all disorders defined by circulating mediators and endothelial injury. On the unfavorable side, sepsis and septic shock, the archetypal cytokine‐storm and endothelial‐injury syndrome, illustrate the opposite lesson. Despite a mechanistic rationale essentially identical to the one advanced here, and despite a small randomized trial suggesting a mortality reduction, the broader evidence for TPE in adult sepsis remains insufficient to establish benefit, and the intervention is not part of standard management. full_text_sections.full_text: Plasma Exchange for Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome: A Mechanistic Case for an Untested Intervention ABSTRACT Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) carries a case fatality rate of 35%–40% and has no approved pharmacologic treatment. Its pathophysiology is rooted in the plasma compartment: cytokines, viral antigens, immune complexes, and platelet‐binding glycoproteins circulate as drivers of immunopathologic endothelial injury, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and cardiogenic depression. Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) achieves bulk clearance of plasma‐borne mediators and is established by the American Society for Apheresis (ASFA) for numerous indications that share an analogous mechanistic rationale. This commentary argues that the immunopathology of HPS maps onto the therapeutic targets of TPE, that any intervention would need to be timed to the early cardiopulmonary phase, and that the coagulopathic dimension of the disease provides a mechanistic argument for incorporating plasma into the replacement strategy. We deliberately situate this rationale against the uneven record of TPE in diseases of comparable pathophysiology, in which the intervention has been effective in some settings and without demonstrable benefit in others. The recent Andes virus outbreak aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, which produced a multinational cluster of severe cardiopulmonary cases, prompted us, as transfusion medicine and apheresis physicians, to articulate this hypothesis. We emphasize that these arguments are mechanistic and hypothesis‐generating rather than evidence‐based: no clinical data yet support TPE in HPS, and systematic outcome reporting, ideally through a multicenter case series, would be required before any conclusion about efficacy could be drawn. Introduction Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), caused primarily by Sin Nombre virus in North America and Andes virus in South America, remains one of the most lethal respiratory infections encountered in the Western Hemisphere. Since its identification following the 1993 Four Corners outbreak, HPS has been characterized by a case fatality rate approaching 35%–40%, a figure that has not materially improved in three decades despite advances in critical care. No antiviral agent has demonstrated efficacy in controlled trials. Ribavirin, the most extensively studied candidate, failed to reduce mortality in a prospective randomized trial and is not recommended for treatment of established HPS. Management remains entirely supportive: mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure, vasopressors for cardiogenic and distributive shock, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) as a rescue strategy in refractory cases . The persistent gap between the severity of this disease and the poverty of its treatment options invites reexamination of established extracorporeal therapies. Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE), a procedure central to transfusion medicine practice and codified in the American Society for Apheresis (ASFA) guidelines for more than 40 indications, has never been formally evaluated or published as a treatment for HPS. This commentary argues that the immunopathology of HPS maps onto the mechanistic rationale for TPE, that the plasma compartment represents a plausible site of actionable pathology, and that the replacement fluid strategy in this context deserves specific attention from a transfusion medicine perspective. We advance these points as a hypothesis to be tested rather than as a recommendation for immediate practice. Two considerations prompted this commentary. The first is mechanistic and is developed below. The second is circumstantial. The 2026 outbreak of Andes virus infection aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, which generated a multinational cluster of hantavirus cardiopulmonary cases with a case fatality ratio within the range historically reported for the disease, returned clinical and public health attention to a syndrome whose therapeutic options have remained essentially static for three decades. We write as transfusion medicine and apheresis physicians rather than as clinicians with first‐hand experience managing HPS, and we are deliberately explicit about that vantage point. Our aim is to frame a mechanistically coherent hypothesis from the perspective of the extracorporeal therapies we practice, so that centers that do encounter these patients, whether in sporadic cases or in the next cluster, are positioned to evaluate and report outcomes systematically. Pathophysiology: The Plasma Compartment as Battlefield Understanding why TPE is mechanistically rational for HPS requires understanding why HPS kills (Figure 1). Hantaviruses infect pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells without inducing direct cytopathic effect. Infected endothelial cells remain architecturally intact; it is the immune response mounted against viral antigens displayed on their surface that destroys the vascular barrier. Cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes, recruited in disproportionate numbers, drive immunopathologic endothelial injury through perforin and granzyme‐mediated mechanisms. The result is not pneumonia in the conventional sense but a diffuse increase in pulmonary vascular permeability, causing protein‐rich fluid to flood the alveolar compartment. The clinical syndrome that follows, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema progressing to refractory hypoxemia within 24–48 h of the cardiopulmonary phase onset, reflects this mechanism precisely. Conceptual rationale for plasma‐directed extracorporeal therapy in hantavirus pulmonary syndrome. TPE and cytokine‐directed extracorporeal therapies are presented as theoretical, hypothesis‐generating approaches; clinical efficacy remains unproven. The cytokine milieu in HPS is the proximate driver of this process. Circulating levels of tumor necrosis factor‐alpha (TNF‐alpha), interleukin‐6 (IL‐6), interleukin‐10 (IL‐10), and interferon‐gamma are markedly elevated in patients with severe disease, correlating with clinical deterioration. These mediators perpetuate endothelial activation, upregulate adhesion molecule expression, and amplify capillary leak beyond the initial viral trigger. Simultaneously, thrombocytopenia, universally observed in HPS, reflects platelet consumption, impaired thrombopoiesis, and direct binding of hantavirus glycoproteins to platelet integrin alpha‐IIb‐beta‐3. Viral antigens and immune complexes circulate during the acute phase, potentially sustaining toll‐like receptor and innate immune activation even as viremia begins to clear. The myocardial depression characteristic of HPS adds a cardiogenic component to what is otherwise a distributive and permeability‐driven shock syndrome. Depressed left ventricular ejection fraction in the acute phase is well described and reflects the effects of circulating mediators on myocardial contractility rather than ischemia or direct viral invasion. This low cardiac output state, superimposed on alveolar flooding from capillary leak, produces the particularly lethal hemodynamic phenotype that distinguishes HPS from other viral pneumonias and has prompted the preferred designation hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). The central observation for the transfusion medicine audience is this: the pathogenic burden in HPS is not primarily cellular or structural. It is humoral. Cytokines, viral antigens, immune complexes, activated complement fragments, and dysfunctional platelet‐binding viral glycoproteins all circulate in plasma. The plasma compartment is both the propagation medium and the therapeutic target. Mechanistic Rationale for Therapeutic Plasma Exchange TPE removes one to one and a half plasma volumes per session, clearing approximately 63%–78% of any given plasma constituent in a single procedure. papers.title: Detection of new world hantaviruses by a broadly reactive rRT-PCR assay.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Orthohantaviruses are negative-sense RNA viruses that persistently infect rodents and can cause severe human disease. Orthohantavirus diversity complicates comprehensive surveillance strategies and diagnostic tools. Currently, serological assays and nested PCR with degenerate primers are used for hantavirus diagnosis and rodent surveillance, but these assays have long turnaround-times. Here, a broadly reactive Orthohantavirus real-time PCR assay is presented that can be incorporated into public health and research laboratories across the Americas. STUDY DESIGN: Starting from an existing rRT-PCR primer-probe set originally developed for the detection of Sin Nombre virus, a pan-America Orthohantavirus assay (HantAmeriQ) was developed that can be used for both human and rodent surveillance. RESULTS: Using synthetic RNA, the HantAmeriQ assay detected all New World Orthohantaviruses known to cause human disease at a limit of detection between 25 (Blue River virus) and 28,000 (Bayou virus) copies/reaction. Genetically diverse hantaviruses from North America (including Sin Nombre, New York, Monongahela, Blue River, and Bayou viruses) and Central/South America (including Catacamas, Carrizal, Choclo, Maciel, and Andes viruses) were detected within similar limits. The HantAmeriQ assay performed as well as or better than a commercially available assay for the detection of North American, but not South American hantaviruses and detected diverse hantaviruses from rodent and human specimens. CONCLUSIONS: Here, the HantAmeriQ assay detected New World Orthohantaviruses in both rodent and human samples from across the United States, and hantaviruses from Central and South America. The assay demonstrates strong potential for diagnostic use in North American clinical laboratories and for surveillance and research applications in rodent-centered field studies.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical virology : the official publication of the Pan American Society for Clinical Virology

papers.title: Artificial intelligence for chest imaging in hantavirus pulmonary syndrome: A review of practical considerations for rare-disease imaging.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) is an uncommon zoonotic respiratory illness with a high case fatality rate. Recent travel-associated Andes orthohantavirus clusters have renewed interest in early radiographic recognition of the disease outside its usual geographic range. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools developed during the COVID-19 pandemic now inform several radiology workflows, but the application of AI to HPS chest imaging remains largely unexplored. This narrative review summarises the imaging features of HPS across modalities, considers lessons from AI applications in COVID-19 and viral pneumonia imaging, and discusses practical development considerations for HPS-aware imaging AI, including dataset development, label standardisation, realistic comparator inclusion, candidate modelling approaches, external validation, and clinical workflow integration. The review also considers challenges to HPS-aware imaging AI, including data scarcity, low pretest probability in non-endemic settings, overlapping imaging findings, and translational pitfalls from recent AI literature. As HPS is unlikely to support conventional disease-specific model development without coordinated data collection, future work will likely require multi-institutional datasets, prevalence-aware evaluation, and multimodal workflow integration that combines imaging with clinical, laboratory, and epidemiologic context.

papers.title_zh: 人工智能在 汉坦病毒肺综合征 胸部影像中的应用:罕见疾病影像的实用考虑综述。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒肺综合征是一种罕见的动物源性呼吸系统疾病,致死率高,亟需改进诊断工具。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述概述了汉坦病毒肺综合征的影像特征,借鉴 COVID-19 人工智能应用的经验,并详细阐述了针对汉坦病毒肺综合征的 AI 开发的实际步骤,包括数据集构建、标签标准化、模型选择、外部验证以及工作流集成。
analysis_zh.current_state: 在 COVID-19 大流行期间开发的 AI 工具已支持众多放射学工作流程,但其在汉坦病毒肺综合征胸部影像中的应用仍基本未被探索。
analysis_zh.gaps: 主要挑战包括数据稀缺、非流行地区的低检前概率、与其他病毒性肺炎影像表现重叠,以及近期 AI 文献中指出的转化陷阱。
analysis_zh.future_research: 未来的进展可能需要协调的多机构数据集、考虑患病率的评估指标,以及将影像与临床、实验室和流行病学数据融合的多模态 AI。

papers.title: Use of tocilizumab for severe hantavirus pulmonary syndrome: a MEURI case series with contextual comparisons.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome is a rare zoonotic disease associated with high mortality, acute respiratory failure, shock, capillary leak, and systemic inflammation. Currently, no specific antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy has proven effective for routine clinical use. The current cruise-associated hantavirus outbreak motivated this early descriptive report from an ongoing, larger, pre-post study (ISRCTN72088243). We aimed to describe tocilizumab use under the Monitored Emergency Use of Unregistered and Investigational Interventions (MEURI) framework. METHODS: In this descriptive case series at Hospital Zonal de Bariloche Dr Ramón Carrillo, San Carlos de Bariloche, Argentina, patients with laboratory-confirmed severe hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission or assessment were eligible to receive tocilizumab in addition to standard supportive care, in accordance with the MEURI framework. Tocilizumab was administered to patients within 24 h of ICU admission or ICU-level evaluation as a single intravenous dose of 8 mg/kg, up to a maximum of 800 mg. During this time, five eligible patients could not receive tocilizumab because timely administration was not feasible due to drug unavailability or refractory shock at diagnosis. This case series represents the first report from the larger, ongoing, pre-post study (ISRCTN72088243). The main descriptive outcome was survival to ICU discharge in patients who received tocilizumab and patients who were eligible to receive tocilizumab but did not. FINDINGS: Between June 1, 2024, and May 5, 2026, 13 patients with laboratory-confirmed hantavirus pulmonary syndrome were evaluated for inclusion after institutional approval of the MEURI protocol. Ten met eligibility criteria for tocilizumab; five received tocilizumab and five did not. In the five eligible non-treated patients, two were diagnosed when they were already in refractory shock, precluding timely administration, and three did not receive tocilizumab because the drug was unavailable when treatment was being considered. Four of five tocilizumab-treated patients survived to ICU discharge. The fifth treated patient died after rapid progression to refractory shock. All five eligible non-treated patients died after ICU admission. INTERPRETATION: These observations suggest that IL-6 inhibition warrants further evaluation within the MEURI framework or analogous expanded-access frameworks, and, when feasible, collaborative randomised studies with standardised data collection. FUNDING: None. TRANSLATIONS: For the Spanish translations of the abstract see Supplementary Materials section.

analysis.background: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome is a rare zoonotic disease with high mortality, acute respiratory failure, shock, capillary leak, and systemic inflammation, and no specific antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy has proven effective for routine use.
analysis.methods: In a descriptive case series at Hospital Zonal de Bariloche, Argentina, laboratory‑confirmed severe HPS patients requiring ICU admission were eligible for tocilizumab (8 mg/kg IV, max 800 mg) within 24 h under the MEURI framework; five eligible patients did not receive the drug due to unavailability or refractory shock, and survival to ICU discharge was the primary outcome.
analysis.results: Between 1 June 2024 and 5 May 2026, 13 patients were evaluated, 10 met eligibility, five received tocilizumab and four survived to ICU discharge while the fifth died; all five eligible non‑treated patients died.
analysis.contribution: This first report from the ongoing study provides observational data suggesting IL‑6 inhibition may improve survival in severe HPS and warrants further evaluation within MEURI or randomized trials.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is available and the small, non‑randomized case series limits causal inference; specific limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome is a rare zoonotic disease with high mortality and no proven specific therapy. Methods: In a descriptive case series at Hospital Zonal de Bariloche, Argentina, severe HPS patients needing ICU care received tocilizumab (8 mg/kg IV) within 24 h under MEURI; five eligible patients did not receive it due to drug unavailability or refractory shock, and survival to ICU discharge was the primary outcome. Results: Of 13 evaluated patients (June 2024–May 2026), ten were eligible, five received tocilizumab (four survived, one died), and all five eligible non‑treated patients died. Contribution: The report provides the first observational evidence that IL‑6 inhibition may improve survival in severe HPS, supporting further evaluation in expanded‑access or randomized studies. Limitations: Only an abstract is available and the small, non‑randomized case series limits causal inference; specific limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒肺综合征 是一种罕见的动物源性疾病,死亡率高,表现为急性呼吸衰竭、休克、毛细血管漏出和全身炎症,且尚无特异性抗病毒或免疫调节疗法被证实可常规使用。
analysis_zh.methods: 在阿根廷巴里洛切地区医院的一项描述性病例系列中,实验室确诊的重症汉坦病毒肺综合征患者需入住ICU,符合条件的患者在MEURI框架下于24小时内接受托珠单抗(8 mg/kg 静脉注射,最大800 mg);因药物缺乏或难治性休克,五例符合条件的患者未接受药物治疗,ICU出院存活率为主要结局指标。
analysis_zh.results: 2024年6月1日至2026年5月5日期间,共评估13例患者,10例符合入组标准,5例接受托珠单抗治疗,其中4例存活至ICU出院,第5例死亡;所有5例未接受治疗的符合条件患者均死亡。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本报告为正在进行的研究的首次报告,提供观察性数据,提示IL‐6抑制可能提升重症汉坦病毒肺综合征的存活率,值得在MEURI框架或随机对照试验中进一步评估。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅有摘要可得,且样本量小、非随机病例系列限制了因果推断;具体局限性未在提供的证据中报告。

papers.title: Hantavirus risk and preparedness in Europe in an era of climate change and global mobility.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonoses causing haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. In Europe, Puumala virus (PUUV) and Dobrava virus (DOBV) account for most recognized disease; Seoul virus (SEOV) is relevant to ports and urban settings. The 2026 MV Hondius cruise-ship cluster of Andes hantavirus (ANDV) infections, involving passengers from 23 countries, has highlighted urgent gaps in European preparedness for both endemic and imported hantavirus disease. OBJECTIVES: To review hantavirus epidemiology, ecology, clinical recognition, diagnostics, and preparedness in Europe, with emphasis on endemic PUUV, DOBV, and SEOV, and to clarify the separate relevance of imported ANDV infection for travel medicine and maritime response. SOURCES: We conducted a structured narrative review of literature published from January 2000 to May 2026, prioritizing surveillance reports, systematic and narrative reviews, rodent ecology studies, diagnostic evaluations, external quality assessment studies, and outbreak investigations. WHO, European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, and International Health Regulations guidance documents were also reviewed. CONTENT: European hantavirus epidemiology is heterogeneous and shaped by reservoir ecology, biome-specific rodent dynamics, clinical awareness, diagnostic capacity, and surveillance practice. Climate effects are indirect and regionally variable, mediated by mast years, predator-prey dynamics, winter conditions, land use, reservoir density, and human exposure. Diagnostic preparedness is uneven, particularly for molecular detection. Imported ANDV infection is rare in Europe but relevant to travel medicine and high-consequence preparedness because it can cause severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and, unlike endemic European hantaviruses, has documented person-to-person transmission. IMPLICATIONS: European preparedness should prioritize PUUV, DOBV, and SEOV through rodent biomonitoring, harmonized surveillance, improved molecular diagnostics, and locally calibrated early warning.
papers.journal: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases

papers.title: Hantavirus infection in emergency radiology: Imaging manifestations, pathophysiology, and infection control considerations.
papers.abstract: In April 2026, several cases of severe respiratory illnesses were reported aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius during its voyage from Argentina. Subsequent laboratory testing identified Andes virus (ANDV), a hantavirus subtype, with rare but documented human-to-human transmission. Although hantavirus infections are uncommon, both hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) are associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Their rapid progression and potential need for intensive respiratory support continue to pose important challenges for emergency departments, intensive care units, and radiology services. Because pulmonary imaging findings often evolve quickly, radiologists play a critical role in early recognition and triage. This review provides an overview of the pathophysiology, imaging manifestations, and operational considerations relevant to hantavirus infection in emergency radiology practice.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 急诊放射学中的感染:影像表现、病理生理学及感染控制考虑。

analysis_zh.background: 近期在一艘邮轮上出现的严重呼吸道疾病病例与 安第斯病毒 相关,该 汉坦病毒 能够进行罕见的人际传播。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述针对汉坦病毒的病理生理学、特征性影像表现以及急诊放射学的运营/感染控制问题。
analysis_zh.current_state: 汉坦病毒感染虽罕见,但汉坦病毒肺综合征和肾综合征出血热导致高发病率和死亡率,肺部影像改变进展迅速。
analysis_zh.gaps: 快速的临床恶化给急诊、重症监护和放射科服务带来挑战,凸显分诊方案和影像指导方面的缺口。
analysis_zh.future_research: 研究应界定最佳影像标准,评估快速响应放射学路径,并评估急诊环境中的感染控制措施。

papers.title: EPIZOOTIC AND EPIDEMIC SITUATION OF HANTAVIRUS INFECTION IN THE WORLD
papers.abstract: This review examines the current epidemiological and epizootic situation in natural foci of hantavirus diseases across various regions of the world. Today, hantavirus diseases represent a significant threat to the sanitary and epidemiological well-being of populations worldwide, capable of seriously complicating the epidemiological situation. Approximately 200,000 cases are registered worldwide annually, although the intensity and dynamics of morbidity vary considerably across regions. In China — the country with the highest annual number of cases in the world — the overall incidence trend is declining. Ukraine is a natural endemic focus for the spread of hantaviruses that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). Given climate change, which stimulates rodent migration and reproduction, epidemiological risks for the rural population and military personnel are increasing. Data on the spread of hantavirus infection in the regions of Southeast Asia and the African continent require further study; however, it is quite evident that hantavirus infection is an underestimated public health problem in these regions, and its true scale — given the wide distribution of reservoir hosts — may be considerably greater than currently known. Keywords: hantavirus diseases, hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, epidemiological situation, natural reservoirs, pathogens.

analysis.background: This review examines the current epidemiological and epizootic situation of hantavirus diseases worldwide, reflecting their significant threat to public health (A1).
analysis.main_directions: It discusses the global burden of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, the role of natural rodent reservoirs, climate‑driven rodent migration increasing risk, and the need for data from Southeast Asia and Africa (A2, A6, A7, A8, A5).
analysis.current_state: Approximately 200,000 cases are reported annually with marked regional variation; incidence is declining in China while Ukraine remains an endemic focus (A3, A4, A5).
analysis.gaps: Surveillance data are limited for many regions, especially Southeast Asia and Africa, leading to likely underestimation of the true disease burden (A7, A8).
analysis.future_research: Enhanced monitoring of rodent hosts, focused epidemiological studies in understudied continents, and evaluation of climate‑change impacts on transmission are recommended (A6, A7, A8).

analysis.summary_en: Background: This review examines the global epidemiological and epizootic situation of hantavirus diseases, a significant public‑health threat. Main directions: It highlights disease burden, natural rodent reservoirs, climate‑driven risk, and data gaps in Southeast Asia and Africa. Current state: About 200,000 cases occur yearly, with declining incidence in China and endemic focus in Ukraine. Gaps: Limited surveillance likely underestimates true burden, especially in understudied regions. Future research: Strengthen rodent surveillance, conduct targeted studies in data‑poor areas, and assess climate‑change effects on transmission.

papers.title: Multi-Country Human-to-Human Andes Virus Outbreak on a Cruise Ship: A Disaster Report on Prehospital, Health Care Facility, and Public Health System Challenges - Essential Knowledge for Frontline Clinicians.
papers.abstract: Abstract The Andes Virus (ANDV) outbreak reported on May 2, 2026, aboard a luxury vessel departing from Ushuaia, Patagonia, Argentina, was caused by an Orthohantavirus unique in its person-to-person transmissibility in contrast to zoonotic transmission characteristic of better-known hantaviruses. Containment required coordinated international management because passengers and crew embarked and disembarked at several international ports-of-call prior to outbreak recognition, resulting in cross-border transmission potential. Among those who disembarked, several traveled on flights to various destinations. Cases subsequently manifested in multiple countries, including Tristan da Cunha, Spain, France, Switzerland, South Africa, Canada, and The Netherlands. Upon notification, international health authorities implemented containment measures, such as contact tracing, quarantine, and isolation. Uniquely, ANDV poses distinctive risks due to its immediately prodromal presymptomatic transmission potential, initial non-specific flu-like symptoms, prolonged incubation period, conceivable long-term neurologic and endocrinologic sequalae, high case fatality rates (CFRs), and possibility of international dissemination. This report describes the successful management of a multi-national outbreak associated with cruise-ship travel, a setting with unique challenges. It also examines implications and challenges for prehospital, health care facility, and public health systems for future ANDV outbreaks. The event was characterized by delayed recognition, international spread, and complex coordination across multiple jurisdictions and sectors, including medical and public health authorities, policy- and decision-makers, crisis and emergency risk-communication experts, media, logistics, transportation, and security. Rapid implementation of public health measures coupled with clinician implementation of the Identify-Isolate-Inform (3I) model, a clinical framework to detect and prevent the spread of infectious disease, at the prehospital and health care facility levels are critical actions that can contain future ANDV outbreaks.

papers.title: Of mice and men: Updates on hantavirus disease and diagnostics.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are a diverse and widespread group of zoonotic viruses under the Orthohantavirus genus that can cause severe acute cardiopulmonary or renal disease. Hantavirus species are grouped generally as either New World or Old World based on geographic distribution, which is influenced by their respective host reservoir including rodents. Although there is no specific treatment for hantaviruses, recognizing clinical presentation and interpreting laboratory results for case identification can improve patient management. Here we review the epidemiology, clinical manifestations, and diagnostic testing options for hantavirus infection.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical virology : the official publication of the Pan American Society for Clinical Virology
